en.abrir:
From Latin ~aperīre~ (“to open, uncover”), which reached Spanish through Vulgar Latin *~operīre~ and Old Spanish ~abrir~. The deeper origin is debated. By the standard account ~aperīre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~apweriō~, analyzed as Proto-Indo-European *~h₂epó~ (“off, away”) plus *~h₂wer-~ (“to cover, shut”) — so “to un-cover” — which would make it a near-mirror of its opposite ~operīre~ (“to cover, close”). This decomposition is plausible but not certain, and other explanations have been proposed. Cognate Romance forms include Italian ~aprire~, Portuguese ~abrir~ and French ~ouvrir~.

Whatever its ultimate source, ~aperīre~ meant “to open” throughout its history, and Spanish ~abrir~ carries that unbroken. Its past participle is the irregular ~abierto~, and from the Latin verb and its relatives Spanish draws ~abertura~ and the learned ~apertura~ (“opening,” as of a chess game or a session), ~abridor~ (“opener”) and ~aperitivo~ (“aperitif” — literally something that “opens” the appetite before a meal). Through French, the same Latin verb gave English ~aperture~ and ~overt~ (from Old French ~ouvert~, “opened”), so an ~overt~ act is, etymologically, an opened one.
en.acabar:
Spanish ~acabar~ was formed within Romance from the noun ~cabo~ (“end, tip, extremity”), with the prefix ~a-~ and the verbal ending ~-ar~; the reconstructed Vulgar Latin form is *~accapāre~. ~cabo~ comes from Latin ~caput~ (“head”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kaput-~ (“head”). That root is cognate, by Grimm’s law (k → h), with English ~head~ and German ~Haupt~; from ~caput~ itself came English ~capital~, ~captain~, and ~chief~. French ~achever~ (“to complete”) and, borrowed from it, English ~achieve~ rest on the same image.

The metaphor is bodily: the ~cabo~ is the “head” or far tip of a thing, so to ~acabar~ is to carry something to its extremity — to finish it off. Spanish put the verb to hard work: ~acabar de~ + infinitive means “to have just” done something, while the phrase ~el acabóse~ names an utter end or a disaster. From ~caput~ the language also drew ~cabeza~ (“head,” via ~capitia~), ~cabecera~ (“headboard, head of a table”), ~cabo~ (the “cape” of a coast and the military “corporal”), ~capital~, and ~capitán~. One Latin word for “head,” then, tops off a Spanish verb for “to end” — and is quietly cognate with the English ~head~ you nod.
en.acercar:
A parasynthetic verb built from ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”), the adverb ~cerca~ (“near”), and the ending ~-ar~ — literally “to make near.” ~cerca~ comes from Latin ~circā~ (“around, round about”), an adverb bound to ~circum~ (“around”) and the noun ~circus~ (“ring, circle”). ~circus~ was most likely taken from, or shared with, Ancient Greek ~kríkos~ / ~kírkos~ (“ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, to bend”); by one account English ~ring~ belongs to the same root.

The semantic hinge is neat: what lies “round about” a spot is precisely what lies “near” it, so Latin ~circā~ “around” slid into Spanish ~cerca~ “nearby,” and the causative ~acercar~ came to mean “to bring closer.” The same word ~cerca~, as a noun, also means a “fence” — that which rings a field — beside the verb ~cercar~ “to encircle, to besiege.” Other kin of the turning-root include ~círculo~, ~circo~, ~circular~, ~cerco~, and the learned dating word ~circa~ itself.
en.acompañar:
From the prefix ~a-~ on ~compañero~/~compaña~, the family goes back to Late Latin ~companio~ (accusative ~companiōnem~), “companion, mess-mate,” a compound of ~com-~ (“with”) and ~pānis~ (“bread”) — literally one who shares bread. This ~companio~ is generally taken as a calque of Proto-West Germanic *~gahlaibō~ (“mess-mate”), first recorded in the Lex Salica, while ~pānis~ itself is traced — with some caution — to Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂-~ (“to feed, protect”). Cognates: Italian ~accompagnare~, French ~accompagner~, English ~accompany~ and ~company~.

The heart of the word is a homely image: a ~companio~ is a “bread-fellow,” the person with whom you break bread. Spanish keeps that warmth in ~compañero~ and ~compañía~, and ~acompañar~ is simply to go alongside someone, to keep them company. The bread at its center, ~pānis~, lives on directly as Spanish ~pan~, and spreads through ~panadería~ (“bakery”) and ~empanada~ (something “breaded,” wrapped in dough).
en.afectar:
From Latin ~affectāre~ (“to strive after, aim at”), the frequentative of ~afficere~ (“to influence, affect”), itself ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~facere~ (“to do, make”). ~facere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~fakiō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, do”). Spanish took the learned ~afectar~ straight from written Latin, yet the very same ~affectāre~ also travelled the popular, spoken road and surfaced as the doublet ~afeitar~ (once “to adorn, to make up,” today simply “to shave”). Cognate with Italian ~affettare~, French ~affecter~, Portuguese ~afetar~, and English ~affect~.

The frequentative sense — to do something repeatedly or pointedly — is why ~afectar~ still splits two ways in Spanish: to affect or influence (« la sequía afectó la cosecha ») and to feign or put on airs (« afectar indiferencia »), the latter preserving the Latin idea of studiously aiming at an effect. The shared root *~dʰeh₁-~ is one of the most fertile in the language, and beyond ~facere~ it seeded ~hacer~, ~hecho~, ~fábrica~, and — through ~afficere~ — the nouns ~afecto~, ~afición~, and ~afectación~.
en.afirmar:
From Latin ~affirmāre~ (“to make firm, strengthen”), from ~ad-~ + ~firmāre~ (“to make firm”), from ~firmus~ (“firm, strong, steadfast”), from Proto-Italic *~fermos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, support”). Cognate with French ~affirmer~, Italian ~affermare~, Portuguese ~afirmar~ and English ~affirm~; through the root, with Sanskrit ~dharma~ (“that which upholds, law, duty”).

To affirm is literally “to make firm” — to hold a statement steady. Latin ~firmus~ gave Spanish a broad family: ~firme~, ~firma~ (a signature, what one holds to), ~firmar~ and ~confirmar~. The negative ~infirmus~ (“not firm, weak”) yielded ~enfermo~ (“sick”), so the sick person is, etymologically, one who has lost firmness. The PIE root *~dʰer-~ also underlies the Indian ~dharma~, the cosmic order that “holds” all things in place.
en.alcanzar:
The origin is debated, but the favored account traces ~alcanzar~ to a Vulgar Latin *~incalciāre~ (“to tread on someone's heels, to pursue”), a verb built on Latin ~calx~ (“heel”). Old Spanish had ~alcanzar~ beside a more transparent ~encalzar~, and the shift of the prefix to ~al-~ is itself uncertain — it may reflect the influence of Latin ~ad~, of the Spanish contraction ~al~, or, by one hypothesis, of the Arabic article ~al-~. Whatever reshaped the head, the Romance kin agree on the body: Portuguese ~alcançar~, Galician ~alcanzar~, and Catalan ~encalçar~ all point back to the same heel-chasing verb.

The image behind the word is vivid: to ~alcanzar~ was first to chase so close that you trod on the runner's ~calx~, his heel — and then, naturally, to catch him, to reach him, to attain your goal. Spanish kept the whole arc of that metaphor, from physical overtaking (« alcanzar la meta ») to abstract achievement (« alcanzar un acuerdo ») to sheer sufficiency (« el dinero no alcanza »). From the same Latin ~calx~ come ~calzar~ (“to put on footwear”), ~calcetín~ (“sock”), ~coz~ (“a kick”), and ~recalcar~ (“to stress, to press down on”).
en.aparecer:
From Latin ~appārēscere~, an inchoative (“to begin to appear”) built on ~appārēre~ (“to appear, to become visible”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~pārēre~ (“to come forth, to be visible”). The ultimate Proto-Indo-European source of ~pārēre~ is uncertain, with more than one reconstruction proposed. Cognate with French ~apparaître~, Italian ~apparire~, and English ~appear~ and ~apparent~.

Latin ~pārēre~ had a second, everyday meaning — “to obey,” to present oneself when summoned — and it seeded a nicely paired set of Spanish verbs. From the plain inchoative ~pārēscere~ came ~parecer~ (“to seem, to appear to be”), while the prefixed ~appārēscere~ gave ~aparecer~ (“to appear, to show up”): to seem is to be merely visible; to appear is to arrive into sight. The family also includes ~aparición~ (“appearance, apparition”), ~aparente~ (“apparent”), and the formal ~comparecer~ (“to appear in court”) — where the old sense of presenting oneself on command still lingers.
en.aplicar:
From Latin ~applicāre~ (“to attach to, to bring toward, to fold onto”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). ~plicāre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”), an enlargement of *~pel-~ (“to fold”). It is cognate with Latin ~plectere~, Ancient Greek ~plékō~ (“I plait”), and, through Germanic, English ~fold~ and ~ply~. The compound survives in Italian ~applicare~, French ~appliquer~, and Portuguese ~aplicar~.

The literal image is of folding one thing onto another; from “laying on” came the figurative “to devote oneself to” and “to put into practice.” The humble root hides a surprise: ~plicāre~ also meant to fold up a ship's sails on nearing the coast, and Vulgar Latin turned that “coming to shore” into a general verb of arrival — the direct source of Spanish ~llegar~ (“to arrive”) and Portuguese ~chegar~. Relatives of the fold-root abound in Spanish: ~plegar~, ~pliegue~, ~plegaria~, ~explicar~, ~complicar~, ~replicar~, and ~emplear~ (from ~implicāre~).
en.aprender:
From Latin ~apprehendere~ (“to seize, grasp”), from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~prehendere~ (“to grasp, take hold of”), itself ~prae-~ (“before”) plus a ~-hendere~ from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰend-~ (“to seize, take”). Cognate with French ~apprendre~, Italian ~apprendere~ and Portuguese ~aprender~; through the same root, with Ancient Greek ~khandánō~ (“to hold, contain”) and — via Germanic — English ~get~.

The mental leap “to seize with the mind” happened already in Latin: ~apprehendere~ moved from grabbing physically to grasping an idea, and by Old French ~aprendre~ that figurative sense was the only one left. So to learn is, etymologically, to “get hold of” knowledge. The learned doublet ~aprehender~ preserves the literal “seize, arrest” meaning. From the same root: ~aprendiz~, ~aprendizaje~, ~comprender~, ~emprender~, ~sorprender~ and ~prender~.
en.asegurar:
From ~a-~ plus ~seguro~ plus the verbal ending ~-ar~ — literally “to make secure.” ~seguro~ comes from Latin ~sēcūrus~ (“free from care, safe”), a compound of ~sē-~ (“without”) and ~cūra~ (“care, concern”). Cognate with French ~assurer~ and ~sûr~, and with English ~secure~ and ~sure~ — the latter two a famous doublet, ~secure~ borrowed straight from Latin and ~sure~ worn down through Old French.

So to assure or ensure is, at root, to remove someone’s cares. The Latin ~sēcūrus~ described a mind at peace, untroubled; from that inner calm the word drifted toward outward safety and reliability. Spanish keeps both threads in ~seguro~, which is at once “safe,” “sure,” and (as a noun) “insurance” — the contract that buys freedom from worry. Relatives include ~seguridad~ (“security”) and, from the same ~cūra~, the verb ~curar~ (“to cure, to care for”) and the noun ~cura~ (“cure,” and also “priest,” the one charged with the care of souls).
en.aumentar:
From Latin ~augmentāre~ (“to increase”), from ~augmentum~ (“growth, increase”), from ~augēre~ (“to increase, enlarge”), from Proto-Italic *~augeō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ewg-~ (“to grow, increase”). Cognate with Italian ~aumentare~, French ~augmenter~, Portuguese ~aumentar~ and English ~augment~; through the root, with English ~eke~ and — via Germanic — ~wax~ (“to grow”).

The PIE root *~h₂ewg-~ was extraordinarily productive in Latin. Beyond ~aumentar~ it gave ~aumento~ and ~auge~ (“peak, height”); through ~auctor~ (“originator, one who makes grow”) came Spanish ~autor~; through ~augustus~ (“consecrated, majestic”), the month ~agosto~ and the name ~Augusto~; and through ~auxilium~ (“help, reinforcement”), ~auxilio~. Even the diviner’s ~augurio~ may belong to this family. To increase is, at bottom, to make something grow.
en.ayudar:
From Latin ~adiūtāre~ (“to help, assist”), the frequentative of ~adiuvāre~, itself ~ad-~ (“toward”) plus ~iuvāre~ (“to help, please”), a verb of uncertain deeper origin. Old Spanish had ~aiudar~ before settling on ~ayudar~. It is cognate with Italian ~aiutare~, Portuguese ~ajudar~ and French ~aider~, and — borrowed through Old French — with English ~aid~ and the learned ~adjutant~.

The frequentative ~adiūtāre~ conveyed repeated or earnest helping, and it is this intensive form, not plain ~iuvāre~, that the Romance languages inherited. Because ~iuvāre~ has no secure Proto-Indo-European pedigree, prudence forbids attaching it to a root here. Within Latin it kept lively company: it was linked to ~iūcundus~ (“pleasant, agreeable”), the source of English ~jocund~. In Spanish the same stem gives ~ayuda~ (“help, aid”), ~ayudante~ (“assistant”) and the learned ~coadyuvar~ (“to contribute, cooperate”), which preserves the ~-iuv-~ that popular ~ayudar~ wore away.
en.añadir:
Spanish ~añadir~ comes, through Old Spanish ~eñadir~ (also ~añader~), from a Vulgar Latin *~innaddere~ or *~inaddere~ — Latin ~addere~ (“to add, put to”) reinforced with the prefix ~in-~. The doubled ~nn~ of the reconstructed form is what Spanish needed to yield the ~ñ~. ~addere~ is itself ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”): literally “to give to, put to.” ~dare~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”), one of the most widespread roots there is — source of Latin ~dōnum~ (“gift”) and Spanish ~dar~, Greek ~dídōmi~ (“I give”), and, via Latin, English ~date~, ~donate~, and ~add~ — the last from ~addere~ itself, the very verb that ~añadir~ elaborates.

The quiet lesson of ~añadir~ is redundancy: Latin ~addere~ already meant “to add” (its ~ad-~ = “to”), yet Vulgar Latin piled a second directional prefix, ~in-~, on top — a doubling-up of “to it” that is exactly what adding feels like. The word’s ~ñ~ is a fossil of the assimilated ~in-~ + ~n~ cluster. Spanish also inherited ~addere~ by the learned road as ~aditar~ (“to add, annotate”) and the nouns ~adición~ (“addition,” including the arithmetic operation) and ~aditivo~ (“additive”). From the broader *~deh₃-~ root come ~dar~, ~dado~ (“die; given”), ~dádiva~ (“gift”), ~donar~, ~perdonar~, and ~dosis~ (from Greek ~dósis~, “a giving”).
en.basar:
From the noun ~base~ (“base, foundation”) plus the verbal ending ~-ar~; ~basar~ is a denominal verb, coined rather than inherited. ~base~ comes from Latin ~basis~ (“base, pedestal”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~βάσις~ (“a step, a stepping, base”), a noun built on the verb ~βαίνω~ (“to go, to step”). That verb descends from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to go, come”) — the same root that, on the Germanic side, produced English ~come~. Romance preserved the Latin noun broadly: Italian ~base~, French ~base~, Portuguese ~base~.

Because ~basar~ was formed on the noun, its story is really the story of ~base~, which moved from the concrete “pedestal, that on which a thing stands” to the abstract “foundation, grounds”; the reflexive ~basarse~ means “to rest on, be grounded in.” A pleasant surprise: the modest Greek ~βαίνω~ (“to step”) also hides inside ~diabetes~ (Greek for “a passing through”) and ~acróbata~ (one who “walks” on the heights). Spanish relatives of ~base~ include ~básico~, ~basamento~, and the chemistry term ~base~.
en.buscar:
Inherited from Old Spanish ~buscar~, but of genuinely uncertain origin — Corominas and the DLE alike label it « de origen incierto ». Several hypotheses compete, none settled. By one account it is tied to ~bosque~ (“forest”), the earliest sense being to beat the woods for game; by another it descends from a Celtic *~boudi~ (“gain, victory”), compared with Old Irish ~búaid~ and Welsh ~budd~. It shares its mystery with cognate Portuguese ~buscar~ and Italian ~buscare~ (“to scrounge, wangle”).

Whatever its source, ~buscar~ had by the medieval period already generalized to “to look for, seek,” and it remains one of the plainest, most frequent verbs in the language. The hunting-in-the-woods story is memorable but rests on the unproven ~bosque~ link, so it is best told as one guess among several rather than as fact. The verb is productive in its own right: it yields ~búsqueda~ and ~busca~ (“search”), ~buscador~ (“search engine; seeker”), ~rebuscar~ (“to search thoroughly”), and the old noun ~buscón~ (“petty crook”), immortalized in Quevedo's picaresque novel ~El Buscón~.
en.caer:
From Latin ~cadere~ (“to fall”), from Proto-Italic *~kadō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱad-~ (“to fall”). The intervocalic ~-d-~ dropped away, giving Old Spanish ~caer~. Cognate with Italian ~cadere~, Portuguese ~cair~ and the now-archaic French ~choir~.

Latin’s ~cāsus~ (“a falling”), the past participle of ~cadere~, became a metaphor for whatever “befalls,” hence Spanish ~caso~ (“case, chance”) and ~casualidad~ (“coincidence”), and grammatical “case.” The setting sun falls: ~ocaso~ (“sunset, decline”) and ~occidente~ (“the West”) come from ~occidere~ (“to fall down, to set”). English borrowed the same verb widely — ~cadence~, ~accident~, ~occasion~, ~decay~ and ~cascade~. Other Spanish descendants: ~caída~, ~decaer~, ~recaer~ and ~cadencia~.
en.cambiar:
From Late Latin ~cambiāre~ (“to exchange, barter”), a term of Gaulish (Celtic) origin, traced to a Gaulish ~cambion~ and a Celtic *~kambos~ (“curved, crooked”), reflecting Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kamb-~ (“to bend, curve”). It is cognate with Italian ~cambiare~, Portuguese ~cambiar~ and French ~changer~, and — through Old French — with English ~change~.

The verb began as commercial jargon: ~cambiāre~ first surfaces in Apuleius, and the noun ~cambium~ (“exchange”) appears only later, in medieval Latin banking. The tie to the Celtic root is engaging but wants care: by one account the sense moved from the physical “to bend, turn” of *~kambos~ to the abstract “to give one thing and turn it into another,” yet this semantic bridge is a proposal, not a documented step. What is secure is the family the verb seeded in Spanish: ~cambio~ (“change, small coin”), ~intercambiar~, ~recambio~ (“spare part”) and, borrowed back through Catalan and Occitan, ~canje~ (“exchange, swap”).
en.celebrar:
From Latin ~celebrāre~ (“to frequent, throng, honor, solemnize”), from ~celeber~ (“much-frequented, crowded, populous; famous”). Cognate with Italian ~celebrare~, French ~célébrer~, Portuguese ~celebrar~ and English ~celebrate~. The deeper origin of ~celeber~ is uncertain; it has been linked to ~celer~ (“swift”), but that connection is unproven and the sources leave the root undetermined, so it is best treated as disputed.

The core image is a crowd: a ~celeber~ place was one thronged with people, and ~celebrāre~ first meant “to fill, to frequent in numbers,” then “to honor with a gathering,” and finally “to solemnize.” A festival is still, etymologically, a well-attended event. The same family gave Spanish ~célebre~ (“famous”), ~celebridad~ and ~celebración~. The oft-repeated claim that ~celeber~ comes from ~celer~ “swift” is appealing but not established — by most accounts the origin remains unknown.
en.cerrar:
Spanish ~cerrar~ comes from Late Latin ~serāre~ (“to bolt, lock, close”), a verb derived from the noun ~sera~ (“a bolt, bar, or lock for a door”). The classical form ~serāre~ appears already in Varro and Tibullus (~serāre forēs~, “to bolt the doors”). Two changes reshaped it in the mouths of speakers. First, the ~-r-~ doubled to ~-rr-~ through confusion with ~serra~ (“saw”) and ~serrāre~ (“to saw”) — an entirely different word — so a Vulgar Latin *~serrāre~ arose, still living as Italian ~serrare~, French ~serrer~ (“to tighten, squeeze”), and Portuguese ~cerrar~. English ~serried~ (as in “serried ranks”) is borrowed from the French. Second, the initial ~s-~ became ~c-~ in Castilian — a shift Corominas attributes to the pull of the near-synonym ~cercar~ (“to enclose”).

So the word’s history hides a small comedy of errors: a verb for locking a door got tangled with the unrelated verb for sawing wood, borrowing its double ~r~, and then swapped its opening consonant under the influence of a synonym. The s-to-c shift is Corominas’s proposal, not a certainty, and is best held as the favored account rather than settled fact. Meaning stayed stable — to shut, close, seal — and Spanish grew a rich brood: ~cerradura~ (“lock”), ~cerrojo~ (“bolt”), ~cierre~ (“closure, zipper”), ~encerrar~ (“to lock up, enclose”), ~cerrado~ (“closed; dense; unintelligible”), and ~cerca~ (“fence,” and the adverb “near”). Beware the false friend: Spanish ~cerrar~ (“to close”) and ~serrar~ (“to saw,” from that same ~serra~) are separate verbs that merely sound alike.
en.comenzar:
From Vulgar Latin *~cominitiāre~, a compound of intensive ~com-~ and ~initiāre~ (“to begin, initiate”), the verb of ~initium~ (“a beginning”). ~initium~ comes from ~inīre~ (“to go in, enter”), from ~in-~ (“in”) plus ~īre~ (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”). Cognate with French ~commencer~, Italian ~cominciare~, Portuguese ~começar~, and Catalan ~començar~; English ~commence~ was borrowed from the Old French form.

The literal core is quietly logical: to begin is to “go into” a thing — ~inīre~ — and ~initium~ named the threshold, the point of entry. Late Latin stacked an intensifying ~com-~ onto ~initiāre~ to make the everyday “start,” and that doubled form, not classical ~incipere~, is what the western Romance languages inherited. Spanish paired the popular ~comenzar~ with the noun ~comienzo~, while borrowing the learned doublets ~iniciar~ and ~inicio~ straight from ~initium~. The same PIE *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”) also underlies ~ir~ itself and words such as ~éxito~ (“exit” of effort → “success”) and ~tránsito~.
en.compartir:
A prefixed compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~partir~ (“to divide, to split”), which comes from Latin ~partīre~ (also deponent ~partīrī~, “to divide, to share out”), from the noun ~pars~, ~partis~ (“part, portion”). ~pars~ descends from Proto-Italic *~partis~; its deeper Proto-Indo-European root is disputed, usually tied to *~per-~ in a sense of apportioning and to the root behind Latin ~pariō~ (“to bring forth”), but no single reconstruction has won out. Compare Italian ~compartire~ and Portuguese ~compartir~, alongside English ~part~ and ~portion~.

Latin ~partīre~ meant to cut a whole into shares; Spanish kept that (“to divide”) but also, through the idea of separating oneself from a place, developed the everyday ~partir~ “to set off, to depart” — the same journey French ~partir~ (“to leave”) completed. Prefixed with ~com-~, the verb means to divide something in common, and so “to share.” The teeming ~pars~ family in Spanish includes ~parte~, ~partido~, ~partícula~, ~partida~, ~repartir~, ~impartir~, and ~apartar~.
en.comprar:
Spanish ~comprar~ descends from Latin ~comparāre~ (“to procure, prepare, get”), through a Vulgar Latin variant *~comperāre~. This ~comparāre~ is ~com-~ (“together, wholly”) plus ~parāre~ (“to prepare, procure, furnish”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to grant, allot”) — the root also behind Latin ~pariō~ (“to bring forth”) and Sanskrit ~pṛṇā́ti~ (“he grants”). The Romance family is unanimous: Portuguese and Catalan ~comprar~, Italian ~comprare~, Romanian ~cumpăra~.

Here lies a genuine trap. Latin had two verbs spelled ~comparāre~: one from ~parāre~ (“to procure”), which became ~comprar~ (“to buy”); the other from ~pār~ (“equal”), meaning “to pair, to match, to compare,” which Spanish later re-borrowed intact as ~comparar~ (“to compare”). The everyday “buy” and the bookish “compare” are thus look-alikes from different Latin bases, not one word split in two. From ~parāre~ Spanish also draws ~preparar~, ~reparar~, ~separar~, ~parar~ (“to stop”), ~aparato~, and the agent noun ~comprador~ (“buyer”); the plain noun ~compra~ (“purchase”) rounds out the set.
en.conocer:
From Old Spanish ~conoçer~, from Vulgar Latin *~cōnōscere~, a reshaping of Latin ~cognōscere~ (“to get to know, recognize”), from ~com-~ (“together, thoroughly”) plus ~gnōscere~/~nōscere~ (“to know”), from Proto-Italic *~gnōskō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know, recognize”). Cognate with Italian ~conoscere~, French ~connaître~, and Portuguese ~conhecer~; through the same root Spanish is kin to English ~know~ and ~cognition~, to Latin-derived ~recognize~ and ~notice~, and to Greek ~gnosis~.

Latin ~cognōscere~ was itself built on ~nōscere~, the simple verb “to know,” with the intensive prefix ~com-~ adding the nuance of coming to know something fully or by acquaintance — which is why Spanish ~conocer~ leans toward knowing a person or place, while ~saber~ covers knowing a fact. The verb’s ~-cer~ ending preserves the Latin inchoative ~-scere~, marking a knowledge that is entered into, a process of becoming acquainted. The same PIE root *~ǵneh₃-~ seeded an enormous Spanish family: ~conocimiento~, ~reconocer~, ~desconocido~, and — through the parallel Latin ~nōscere~/~nōtus~ — ~noticia~, ~nota~, ~notar~, and ~noble~ (“knowable, well-known”).
en.conseguir:
From Latin ~consequī~ (“to follow after, to pursue, to attain”), from intensive ~com-~ plus ~sequī~ (“to follow”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). It is a learned or semi-learned relative of the inherited ~seguir~ (directly from ~sequī~). Through the same root come Italian ~conseguire~, English ~sequence~, ~consequence~, ~second~, and ~pursue~, and — from the Greek branch — ~hépomai~ (“to follow”).

The logic of “to obtain” is a small chase: ~consequī~ meant to follow something all the way through until you reach it, so “to attain” is simply “to follow to the end.” Spanish keeps that hunting sense sharp in ~perseguir~ (“to pursue, persecute”) and ~conseguir~ (“to get, to manage to”), where the prize is whatever you have chased down. From the same *~sekʷ-~ Spanish also has ~seguir~, ~consecuencia~ (“that which follows”), ~consecutivo~, ~secuencia~, and ~séquito~ (“retinue,” the followers of a great person) — a whole vocabulary built on the simple act of coming after.
en.considerar:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~cōnsīderāre~ (“to look at closely, examine, weigh”), cognate with Italian ~considerare~, French ~considérer~, Portuguese ~considerar~, and English ~consider~. The word is traditionally parsed as ~con-~ (an intensifying prefix) plus a stem tied to ~sīdus~ (stem ~sīder-~, “star, constellation”) — but this is only a proposal: the sources hedge it as « perhaps » from ~sīdus~, and ~sīdus~ itself is of uncertain origin.

By that appealing hypothesis, ~cōnsīderāre~ was once an augur's or astronomer's term meaning “to observe the stars attentively,” paired with ~dēsīderāre~ (“to cease watching the stars,” hence “to long for, miss”), the source of Spanish ~desear~ and English ~desire~. It is a lovely story — attention to the heavens becoming careful thought — but because the ~sīdus~ link is unproven, it should be offered as a guess, not a fact. What is secure is the classical sense already present in Latin: to examine, to weigh in the mind. From ~cōnsīderāre~ Spanish drew ~consideración~ (“consideration”), ~considerable~, ~considerado~ (“considerate”), and ~desconsiderado~ (“inconsiderate”).
en.construir:
Spanish ~construir~ comes from Latin ~cōnstruere~ (“to heap up, build, construct”), a compound of the prefix ~con-~ (“together”) and ~struere~ (“to pile up, arrange, build”). ~struere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~strew-~ (“to spread, strew”), the same root that, in the Germanic line, gave English ~strew~ and ~straw~ (originally “that which is strewn”). The Latin verb seeded a large family: ~īnstruere~ (“to build in, equip, teach”), ~dēstruere~ (“to un-build, destroy”), and the noun ~strūctūra~. English took ~construct~, ~structure~, ~instrument~, and ~destroy~ from these; Italian has ~costruire~, French ~construire~, and Portuguese ~construir~.

The image at the root is spreading things out in layers — laying courses one over another — so ~construere~ literally piled materials together into a structure. Spanish inherited the verb with an irregular twist: the ~-uir~ conjugation inserts a ~-y-~ before an ending that begins with a strong vowel (~construyo~, ~construyó~, ~construyendo~), a pattern shared by ~huir~ and ~destruir~. Beyond building, ~construir~ serves grammar (~construir una frase~, “to construct a sentence”) and geometry. From the same root Spanish keeps ~estructura~, ~construcción~, ~instruir~, ~instrumento~, ~destruir~, and ~industria~ — the last, by one account, from ~indu-~ (“within”) plus a ~struere~ element, though that derivation is debated.
en.consultar:
From Latin ~consultāre~ (“to deliberate, take counsel repeatedly”), the frequentative of ~consulere~ (“to take counsel, consult”). Cognate with Italian ~consultare~, French ~consulter~ and English ~consult~ and ~counsel~. The origin of ~consulere~ is debated: de Vaan takes it as the primary verb (not derived from ~consul~) — probably ~com-~ (“together”) plus a root meaning “gather,” so “to call the Senate together.”

However ~consul~ and ~consulere~ are ultimately related, the shared image is people brought together to deliberate. From ~consilium~ (“counsel, deliberation”) Spanish drew ~consejo~ (“advice, council”) and ~consejero~; from the verb come ~consulta~, ~consultor~ and ~consultorio~, and the ancient title ~cónsul~. To consult, then, is to gather minds — whether around a doctor, a lawyer, or a book.
en.contar:
From Latin ~computāre~ (“to reckon, to calculate”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~putāre~ (“to reckon, to think; originally to prune, to clean up”). Through Vulgar Latin the word wore down to Old Spanish ~contar~. Its Romance kin are Italian ~contare~ and Portuguese ~contar~; French split it into two spellings, ~compter~ (“to count”) and ~conter~ (“to tell”). English ~count~ came through Old French, while the undamaged Latin form re-entered as the learned doublet ~compute~.

The double life of the verb is the memorable part: ~contar~ means both “to count” and “to tell, to narrate,” exactly as English pairs ~count~ with ~recount~ and French pairs ~compter~ with ~conter~ — to enumerate and to recount are the same act of running through items in order. Spanish keeps both alive in ~cuenta~ (“a bill, an account”) and ~cuento~ (“a tale, a story”). Other kin include ~contador~ (“accountant; meter”), ~contable~, ~descontar~ (“to discount”), and the learned ~cómputo~ (“computation”) and ~computadora~ (“computer”).
en.continuar:
From Latin ~continuāre~ (“to join, to make continuous”), from the adjective ~continuus~ (“uninterrupted, hanging together”), from ~continēre~ (“to hold together”), which is ~con-~ (“together”) + ~tenēre~ (“to hold”). ~tenēre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~tenēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, to draw”). The stretching sense links it, across the family, to Ancient Greek ~teínō~ (“I stretch”) and Sanskrit ~tanóti~ (“he stretches”). Cognate Romance verbs include Italian ~continuare~, French ~continuer~, and Portuguese ~continuar~.

The metaphor hidden in ~continuar~ is textile: something ~continuus~ is a thread held together without a break, so to continue is literally to keep the thread taut and unbroken. That same *~ten-~ runs through a remarkable range of Spanish words — ~tener~, ~tenso~, ~tienda~ (a “tent,” a stretched cloth, and by extension a “shop”), ~tono~, ~contener~, and ~mantener~. Curiously, the “stretch” root even reaches ~tenue~ (“thin, faint”), a thing stretched until it is fine.
en.convertir:
Spanish ~convertir~ derives from Latin ~convertere~ (“to turn around, transform”), from the prefix ~con-~ and ~vertere~ (“to turn”). ~vertere~ rests on Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn, rotate”), a root richly attested across the family: Sanskrit ~vártate~ (“it turns”), German ~werden~ (“to become”) and the English suffix ~-ward~ (as in “toward,” a turning in some direction) all descend from it.

To convert is, at heart, to turn something into something else — a religious “conversion” is a turning of the soul, and ~convertir~ keeps that pivot of transformation. Spanish inherited ~vertere~ directly as ~verter~ (“to pour, spill”), and built a wide prefixed family: ~invertir~ (“to invert; to invest”), ~advertir~ (“to warn, to notice”), ~divertir~ (“to divert; to amuse”) and ~revertir~ (“to revert”), alongside the nouns ~verso~ (“verse,” a line that turns) and ~versión~.
en.crear:
From Latin ~creāre~ (“to create, produce, bring forth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱer-~ (“to grow, become bigger”). The same root produced Latin ~crēscere~ (“to grow”) and the grain-goddess ~Cerēs~, whose name gave us ~cereal~. Cognate Romance descendants include Italian ~creare~, Portuguese ~criar~ and French ~créer~; English ~create~ is a learned borrowing of the Latin participle ~creātus~.

The Latin verb tied creating to growing and bringing forth, and Spanish kept both threads: ~crear~ means “to create,” while its inherited doublet ~criar~ means “to raise, rear, breed” — to make something grow. From the same root Spanish draws ~creación~, ~creador~, ~criatura~ (“creature”) and ~criadero~ (“breeding ground”), and, through ~crēscere~, the growth family ~crecer~, ~creciente~ and ~incremento~. English shares the harvest: ~create~ and ~creature~, but also ~crescent~ (a “growing” moon), ~increase~ and even ~recruit~ — originally a fresh “growth” of new soldiers.
en.creer:
From Old Spanish ~creer~ (also ~creder~), from Latin ~crēdere~ (“to believe, trust, entrust”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱred-dʰeh₁-~ (“to place one’s heart”), a compound of *~ḱḗr~ (“heart”) and *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place”). Cognate with Italian ~credere~, French ~croire~, and Portuguese ~crer~; through the same Latin verb English gained ~creed~, ~credo~, ~credit~, and ~credible~. The first element is the same *~ḱḗr~ that gave Latin ~cor~ and English ~heart~ and ~cardiac~.

The etymology is unusually vivid: to believe was, literally, to “put your heart” into something — the same gesture of trust that lets ~crēdere~ mean both “believe” and, in commerce, “lend on trust,” the source of ~credit~. Latin ~crēdere~ took the dative of the person trusted, and Spanish still says ~creer a alguien~ (“to believe someone”) beside ~creer en~ (“to believe in”). The heart-root *~ḱḗr~ hides inside a surprising crowd of Spanish words: ~creencia~, ~crédito~, ~credo~, ~increíble~, ~credencial~, and ~credibilidad~, while its “heart” sense survives directly in ~cordial~, ~acordar~, and ~recordar~ (“to remember,” literally to bring back through the heart).
en.cumplir:
From Latin ~complēre~ (“to fill up, complete, fulfill”), from ~com-~ (intensive) plus ~plēre~ (“to fill”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”). Medieval Spanish had ~complir~ before ~cumplir~ prevailed. It is cognate with Portuguese ~cumprir~ and, through the same Latin verb, with English ~complete~, ~comply~ and ~compliment~; the bare root surfaces in English ~full~ and ~fill~.

The sense ran from “to fill up” to “to fulfill, discharge, carry out (a duty).” Two byways are memorable. First, the phrase ~cumplir años~ (“to complete years”) produced ~cumpleaños~ (“birthday”). Second, the courtesy sense of ~complēre~ passed through Italian ~complimento~ to give both Spanish ~cumplido~ and, back in English, ~comply~ and ~compliment~ — once, to ~comply~ was simply to be gracious. From the same root Spanish keeps the popular ~lleno~ (“full,” from ~plēnus~) beside the learned ~pleno~, along with ~completo~ and ~complemento~.
en.dar:
Spanish ~dar~ descends straight from Latin ~dare~ (“to give”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”) — one of the most stable meanings in the whole family. The same root shines through Latin ~dōnum~ (“gift”), Greek ~dídōmi~ (“I give”), and Sanskrit ~dádāti~. Italian ~dare~ and Portuguese ~dar~ kept the plain verb, but French abandoned it for ~donner~ (from ~dōnāre~, “to make a gift”), leaving Spanish among the languages that still simply “give” with ~dare~.

For so short a verb, ~dar~ carries an enormous idiomatic load in Spanish, while its root branches out into a whole family of giving. The language has ~dádiva~ (“gift”), ~don~ (“gift, talent”) and ~donar~ (“to donate”), and, through the Latin participle, ~dado~ (“given; a die”) and ~dato~ (“fact, datum”). Even English ~date~ and ~data~, borrowed from the same Latin participle ~datum~ (“given”), belong to this quietly generous root.
en.deber:
Spanish ~deber~ comes from Latin ~dēbēre~ (“to owe”), which began as a contraction of ~dē-~ (“from, away”) plus ~habēre~ (“to have”): to owe was “to have something from someone else,” held but not truly one's own. So ~deber~ is, at root, a compound of ~haber~. Its Romance siblings share it: French ~devoir~, Italian ~dovere~, Portuguese ~dever~. English ~debt~ and ~due~ come from the same Latin verb, borrowed through French, so they are cousins rather than natives.

From “owe,” ~deber~ grew a second, modal life: to owe an action is to be obliged to do it, so ~deber~ came to mean “must, ought” — ~debo irme~ (“I must go”). The noun ~deber~ means “duty,” and ~deberes~ are a schoolchild's “homework,” obligations owed. The financial thread survives in ~débito~ (“debit”), ~deuda~ (“debt”), and ~debido~ (“due, owed”) — the whole family circling the idea of something held that must be given back.
en.decidir:
From Latin ~dēcīdere~ (“to cut off, to determine”), from ~dē-~ (“off, away”) plus ~caedere~ (“to cut, to strike down”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kh₂eyd-~ (“to strike, to cut”). Cognate with French ~décider~, Italian ~decidere~, and English ~decide~ and ~decision~.

The metaphor is a blade: to decide is to cut off deliberation, severing every alternative but the chosen one — the mental equivalent of slicing through a knot. ~caedere~ was a violent, physical verb, and it left a bloody trail across Latin: it is the ~-cide~ of ~homicida~ (“murderer”) and ~suicidio~, literally acts of cutting down. Gentler siblings survive in Spanish too: from ~praecīdere~ (“to cut in front”) came ~preciso~ and ~precisar~ (“precise,” cut to exact measure), and from ~concīdere~ came ~conciso~ (“concise,” cut short). Every ~decisión~, then, is a small cut.
en.decir:
Spanish ~decir~ comes, through Old Spanish ~dezir~, from Latin ~dīcere~ (“to say, to tell”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”) — saying imagined first as pointing something out. That root of showing gave, on the Germanic side, English ~teach~ and ~token~, and in Greek ~deíknymi~ (“I show”). The Romance reflexes stayed close: Italian ~dire~, French ~dire~, Portuguese ~dizer~.

The step from “point out” to “speak” is the whole story of the word, and the pointing sense lingers in its relatives. Spanish keeps the past participle ~dicho~ (“said; a saying”) and builds ~contradecir~ (“to contradict”) and ~bendecir~ (“to bless,” literally “to say well”). From the same root come ~dictar~ (“to dictate”) and ~dictado~, the legal ~edicto~ (“edict”), and ~índice~ (“index, forefinger”) — the very finger that points.
en.dedicar:
From Latin ~dedicāre~ (“to consecrate, to dedicate, to proclaim”), from ~de-~ (“completely, down”) + ~dicāre~ (“to proclaim solemnly, to consecrate”). ~dicāre~ is a first-conjugation relative of ~dīcere~ (“to say”), and both go back to Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”). That root surfaces in Ancient Greek ~deíknumi~ (“I show”), German ~zeigen~ (“to show”), and English ~teach~ and ~token~. Spanish took the learned ~dedicar~ from Latin. Cognate with Italian ~dedicare~, French ~dédier~, and Portuguese ~dedicar~.

The root idea is pointing: to ~dicāre~ was to point something out with words, to proclaim it — and to ~dedicāre~ was to point it out entirely, to set it apart by solemn declaration, as a temple was dedicated to a god. Modern ~dedicar~ keeps that sense of setting time or effort apart for a purpose. The pointing root *~deyḱ-~ is astonishingly productive in Spanish: ~decir~, ~índice~ (“the pointing finger”), ~dedo~ (“finger”), ~juez~ and ~juzgar~ (“to point out the law,” ~ius~ + ~dicere~), ~predecir~, and ~dictar~.
en.dejar:
From Old Spanish ~dexar~ (also ~lexar~), from Latin ~laxāre~ (“to loosen, slacken, let go”), the denominative verb of ~laxus~ (“loose, slack”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)leg-~ (“to be slack”). Cognate with Portuguese ~deixar~, French ~laisser~, and Italian ~lasciare~, all of which kept the original ~l-~; through the same Latin verb English acquired ~relax~, ~release~, and ~lease~, and through the same PIE root the native English ~slack~.

Latin ~laxāre~ first meant to slacken a rope or relax the limbs; in Ibero-Romance the sense drifted to “let go,” then “leave behind, allow.” The startling feature of the Spanish form is its initial ~d-~: by one commonly cited account, the expected ~l-~ shifted to ~d-~ under the pull of ~dar~ (“to give”), a neighbor in both meaning and grammar — a swap that sets ~dejar~ apart from its ~l-~-keeping cousins. First documented around 1140, it later spread from “leave” into “stop” and “let.” The same Latin verb seeded the learned Spanish ~laxo~, ~laxante~, and ~relajar~ (a bookish doublet of ~dejar~), plus ~dejadez~ (“lassitude, neglect”).
en.demostrar:
Spanish ~demostrar~ comes from Latin ~dēmōnstrāre~ (“to point out, indicate, prove”), a compound of ~dē-~ (“fully, from”) and ~mōnstrāre~ (“to show, point out”). ~mōnstrāre~ is a denominal verb from ~mōnstrum~ — originally “a divine omen, a portent” — which in turn derives from ~monēre~ (“to warn, advise, remind”). ~monēre~ reflects Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”), the vast root behind Latin ~mēns~ (“mind”) and English ~mind~, ~mental~, and ~mean~. English took ~demonstrate~, ~monster~, ~monstrance~, and ~monitor~ from this branch. Italian ~dimostrare~, French ~montrer~ / ~démontrer~, and Portuguese ~demonstrar~ are the Romance parallels of ~demostrar~.

The buried surprise is ~mōnstrum~: a monster was first not a beast but a sign — something shown by the gods as a warning, from ~monēre~ (“to warn”). A ~mōnstrum~ was a portent that pointed to something, and ~mōnstrāre~ meant to point it out; ~dēmōnstrāre~ intensified this into showing thoroughly, and thence proving. Spanish split the inheritance: popular ~mostrar~ evolved by regular sound change, while learned ~demostrar~ was reborrowed closer to the Latin. From the same ~monēre~ / *~men-~ family Spanish keeps ~mostrar~, ~muestra~ (“sample, sign”), ~monstruo~, ~amonestar~ (“to admonish”), ~mente~, and ~mención~.
en.desarrollar:
A Spanish formation from ~des-~ (a prefix of reversal) and ~arrollar~ (“to roll up”), which is ~a-~ plus ~rollo~ (“a roll, scroll”). ~rollo~ descends from Latin ~rotulus~ (“little wheel, roll”), the diminutive of ~rota~ (“wheel”), from Proto-Indo-European *~Hret-~ (“to run, to roll”). The wheel-root has far-flung cognates: German ~Rad~ (“wheel”), Sanskrit ~rátha~ (“chariot”), and Old Irish ~roth~ (“wheel”); ~rotulus~ itself gave English ~roll~ and ~role~ through French ~rôle~.

The image is vivid and exact: to develop is literally to un-roll — ~des-~ + ~arrollar~ — as one opens a rolled scroll to reveal what is written inside. Growth, in this metaphor, is a scroll unspooling. English ~develop~ carries the very same picture by a different route (Old French ~desveloper~, “to unwrap”), so the two languages independently imagine progress as undoing a wrapping. From the same wheel-root Spanish keeps ~rollo~, ~arrollar~, ~rueda~ (“wheel,” straight from ~rota~), ~rótula~ (“kneecap”), and the borrowed ~rotación~ and ~control~ (via the roll-counter of French ~contre-rôle~).
en.desear:
From Latin ~dēsīderāre~ (“to long for, miss, feel the want of”), traditionally analyzed as ~dē-~ + ~sīdus~ (stem ~sīder-~, “star, constellation”), and inherited by Old Spanish as ~desear~. Cognate with Italian ~desiderare~ and Portuguese ~desejar~, and — through the noun ~dēsīderium~ — with English ~desire~ (via Old French).

The star etymology is the classic account, pairing ~dēsīderāre~ with ~cōnsīderāre~ (“to observe the stars closely”): to desire would be to note a star’s absence, to long for what is no longer in sight. But this is disputed — some scholars reject the ~sīdus~ connection outright and derive the verb from a root meaning “stretch, survey,” so the celestial story, charming as it is, should be taken as one proposal, not settled fact. Secure descendants include ~deseo~, ~deseable~ and ~desiderátum~; from ~sīdus~ itself come ~sideral~ and ~considerar~.
en.destacar:
A comparatively late loan: Spanish took ~destacar~ from French ~détacher~ (“to detach”), from Old French ~destachier~, the negative counterpart of ~atachier~ (“to attach”). French itself leaned on Italian ~staccare~ / ~distaccare~ (“to separate”), the antonym of ~attaccare~ (“to attach, join battle”). At the base lies a Germanic (Frankish) *~stakka~ (“stake, post”), the same source that gave Spanish ~estaca~ (“stake”). It entered Spanish dictionaries around 1705, cognate with English ~detach~.

The oldest sense was military: to ~destacar~ was to detach a body of troops from the main force. From “separate a part from the whole” grew the figurative “stand out, be conspicuous” — that which is set apart draws the eye. The very pair survives elsewhere in Spanish: ~atacar~ (“to attack”), taken from the ~attaccare~ side of the same Italian opposition, once meant “to join, engage.” Modern relatives include ~destacamento~ (“military detachment”), ~destacado~ (“prominent, outstanding”) and the shared ~estaca~.
en.determinar:
Spanish ~determinar~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dētermināre~ (“to set bounds, mark off”), a compound of ~dē-~ (here intensive) and ~termināre~ (“to limit”), a verb on the noun ~terminus~ (“boundary, limit”). ~terminus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~termnos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~térmn̥~ (“boundary marker”), cognate with Ancient Greek ~τέρμα~ (térma, “goal, turning-post”) and ~τέρμων~ (térmōn, “border”). English took the same Latin word as ~determine~; ~term~ and ~terminal~ share the root.

The metaphor at the heart of the verb is spatial: to ~determinar~ is to draw a line around something, and by fixing its edges to fix what it is — hence the senses “to establish,” “to decide,” and “to cause.” The boundary was no small matter to the Romans: ~Terminus~ was a god, the deity of boundary stones, whose markers were sacred and whose festival, the ~Terminalia~, was kept each February. From the same root Spanish inherited ~término~ (“term, end”), ~terminar~ (“to finish”), ~terminal~, ~exterminar~, ~interminable~, and ~determinación~. To determine something, then, is to give it a ~terminus~ — an end that defines its beginning.
en.dirigir:
Spanish ~dirigir~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dīrigere~ (“to set straight, guide, direct”), a compound of ~dis-~ (“apart, asunder”) and ~regere~ (“to keep straight, rule, guide”). ~regere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, direct, rule”), one of the most productive of all roots, cognate with Latin ~rēx~ (“king”), Sanskrit ~rājan~ (“king”), German ~recht~ (“right”), and English ~right~ itself. French ~diriger~ and Italian ~dirigere~ are the Romance parallels.

The literal image is a straight line: to ~dirigir~ is to make something go straight toward a target — hence “to aim,” “to guide,” “to address (a letter),” and “to conduct or manage” an orchestra, a company, a film. Its popularly inherited cousin ~aderezar~ (“to season, to garnish, to set right”), worn smooth by ordinary transmission from the same Latin stock, stands beside the bookish, near-intact ~dirigir~. From ~regere~ and its root Spanish drew a rich harvest: ~regir~ (“to govern”), ~dirección~, ~director~, ~corregir~ (“to correct,” literally “to set right again”), ~erigir~, ~recto~ (“straight”), ~regla~ (“rule”), ~región~, and — presiding over them all — ~rey~ (“king”).
en.disfrutar:
Spanish ~disfrutar~ was formed within Spanish itself from the prefix ~dis-~ and ~fruto~ (“fruit, produce”), with the verbal ending ~-ar~. ~fruto~ comes from Latin ~frūctus~ (“fruit, produce, profit”), the past participle of the deponent verb ~fruī~ (“to enjoy, have the use of”). That verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰruHg-~ (“to make use of, enjoy”). The root surfaces widely: Latin ~frūx~ (“crop, fruit”) gave ~frūgālis~, source of English ~frugal~; and through the Germanic branch it yielded English ~brook~ (the verb “to tolerate, put up with,” originally “to make use of, enjoy”) and German ~brauchen~ (“to need, use”). French ~fruit~ and Portuguese ~fruto~ / ~desfrutar~ are close Romance kin.

The metaphor is agricultural: to ~disfrutar~ something was first to draw the fruits or profit from it — to reap the yield of an estate — and only afterward to enjoy it in the modern sense of taking pleasure. Old legal Spanish kept the concrete meaning of usufruct, the right to gather another’s produce, and the doublet ~usufructo~ still names it in law. Today ~disfrutar de la vida~ (“to enjoy life”) has fully abstracted the harvest into pleasure. From the same ~fruto~ family Spanish holds ~fruta~, ~fructífero~ (“fruitful”), ~usufructo~, and ~frugal~; the learned ~fruición~ (“keen enjoyment”) comes straight from ~fruī~’s participle ~fruitus~.
en.disponer:
Spanish ~disponer~ continues Latin ~dispōnere~ (“to arrange, set in order, distribute”), a compound of ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) and ~pōnere~ (“to place, put”). ~pōnere~ is itself contracted from an older ~po-~ (a by-form of the prefix meaning “away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, leave”), so its literal weight is “to set down, put in place.” The Romance cognates are exact — Italian ~disporre~, French ~disposer~, Portuguese ~dispor~ — and English ~dispose~ arrived through Old French.

The prefix ~dis-~ paints the picture: to ~disponer~ is to place things about, each in its own spot — hence “to arrange” and, from having things arranged and ready, “to have at one’s disposal.” The reflexive ~disponerse a~ means to get ready to do something. ~pōnere~ is one of the great Latin verb-factories, and Spanish reflects it everywhere: ~poner~ (“to put”), ~componer~, ~exponer~, ~proponer~, ~suponer~, ~posición~, ~puesto~, and the derived noun ~disposición~ (“arrangement, disposal, willingness”). The adjective ~disponible~ (“available”) carries the same idea — something set out and ready to hand.
en.elegir:
From Latin ~ēligere~ (“to pick out, to choose”), from ~ex-~ (“out of”) + ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick, to read”). ~legere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~legō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, to collect”). The same root gave Ancient Greek ~légō~ (“I gather, I say”), the ancestor of ~-logy~ and ~logic~. Old Spanish inherited the verb as ~esleer~/~eslecher~ before the learned ~elegir~ reshaped it on the Latin model. Cognate with Italian ~eleggere~, French ~élire~, and Portuguese ~eleger~.

~legere~ began concretely — to gather up, as one gathers olives or firewood — and then specialized in two directions: to gather written signs with the eye (“to read”) and to gather out the best (“to choose,” with ~ex-~). Spanish ~elegir~ keeps only the choosing sense, and its past participle ~electo~ gave the political ~elección~ and ~electorado~. The gathering root *~leǵ-~ also seeded ~leer~ (“to read”), ~colegio~, ~coleccionar~, ~legión~, and ~inteligente~ (“one who chooses between,” ~inter-~ + ~legere~).
en.empezar:
Spanish ~empezar~ is a compound of the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and the noun ~pieza~ (“piece”) — some accounts reconstruct an intervening Vulgar Latin *~impettiāre~, though that form is only proposed, not attested. What is clear is the ~pieza~ at its core, and ~pieza~ is not Latin: it comes from Late Latin ~pettia~, borrowed from Gaulish *~pettyā~, from Proto-Celtic *~kʷezdis~. So one of Spanish's common verbs for “to begin” has a Celtic heart. Its Romance kin through ~pieza~ include French ~pièce~, Italian ~pezza~ and Portuguese ~peça~.

The image behind ~empezar~ is concrete and homely: to begin something is to break into it — to break off the first ~pieza~, to broach a whole. You start a loaf or a task by taking the first piece of it. From the same Celtic-derived ~pieza~ Spanish built ~despiezar~ (“to dismantle, to break into pieces”) and the noun ~empiece~ (“a beginning”), while ~pieza~ itself ranges from a coin to a room to a musical or theatrical piece. It is a small monument to the Gaulish substrate embedded in everyday Castilian.
en.encontrar:
From Vulgar Latin *~incontrāre~ (“to meet, to come up against”), a verb built from Latin ~in-~ (“in, upon”) plus ~contrā~ (“against, facing”), itself from ~cum~ / ~com-~ (“with”). Old Spanish inherited it as ~encontrar~. Its Romance relatives include Italian ~incontrare~, Portuguese ~encontrar~, and French ~encontrer~ (surviving today mainly in ~rencontrer~, “to meet”); English borrowed the same formation as ~encounter~ and, more plainly, ~counter~.

The literal core is confrontational — to come face to face, even against one another — but Spanish softened the edge: ~encontrar~ is now the neutral, everyday verb both for meeting a person and for finding a thing (« no encuentro las llaves »). The reflexive ~encontrarse~ adds “to be located” and “to feel” (« me encuentro bien »). From the same stem come the noun ~encuentro~ (“a meeting, a match”), the blunt ~encontronazo~ (“a collision, a run-in”), and, through the shared ~contrā~, a whole regiment of words — ~contra~, ~contrario~, ~encontrado~ (“opposing, conflicting”), and ~contrariar~.
en.entender:
From Latin ~intendere~ (“to stretch toward, direct, aim at”), formed from ~in-~ (“toward”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, extend”). It is cognate with Italian ~intendere~, Portuguese ~entender~ and French ~entendre~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~intend~; the bare root shows up in English ~tend~ and ~thin~.

The Latin phrase ~intendere animum~ meant “to direct the mind toward” something; that mental aiming narrowed from “pay attention” to “grasp, understand.” A neat contrast: French ~entendre~ took the same verb and settled on “to hear” instead. The root *~ten-~ is remarkably fertile in Spanish: besides ~atender~ (“to attend to”) and ~intención~, it yields ~tensión~, the Greek-derived ~tono~, and — unexpectedly — ~tienda~ (“shop; tent”), originally a “stretched” awning under which goods were sold.
en.entrar:
Spanish ~entrar~ comes, through Old Spanish ~entrar~, from Latin ~intrāre~ (“to go in, enter”), a verb built on ~intrā~ (“within, inside”). ~intrā~ is the feminine ablative of an adjective going back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁énteros~ (“inner”), a comparative formed from *~h₁én~ (“in”) with the contrastive suffix *~-teros~. The word thus meant, quite literally, to move into the more-inner space. English ~enter~ (borrowed through Old French ~entrer~) and Italian ~entrare~ are close relatives, as are Portuguese and Catalan ~entrar~.

The Latin sense was concrete and spatial, and Spanish ~entrar~ keeps that physical core — to enter a room, a country, a stage — while branching into countless idioms: ~entrar en razón~ (“to see reason”), ~entrar en calor~ (“to warm up”), the new year that ~entra~. From the same ~intrā~/~inter~ stock Spanish holds ~entrada~ (“entrance, ticket”), ~entrante~ (“incoming; starter course”), and ~adentro~; the sister preposition ~inter~ underlies ~interior~, ~íntimo~, and ~entre~ (“between”) itself. The comparative shape of *~h₁énteros~ — “more inward” — reminds us that Latin often located actions not just in space but along a scale of depth.
en.enviar:
Spanish ~enviar~ comes from Old Spanish ~enviar~, from Late Latin ~inviāre~ (“to send on a journey, dispatch”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in, on”) and ~via~ (“way, road”). To ~inviāre~ was literally to put someone or something ~in viam~ — “on the road.” ~via~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~weǵʰ-~ (“to go, transport in a vehicle”), one of the great roots of the family: it gave Latin ~vehere~ (“to carry”) and English ~way~, ~weigh~, ~wain~, and ~wagon~, plus the borrowings ~via~, ~vehicle~, and ~voyage~. French ~envoyer~ is the exact cognate — and English ~envoy~ (“a messenger”) is simply its past participle ~envoyé~ borrowed whole.

The metaphor is transparent and durable: sending is still, etymologically, a matter of setting something on its way. From ordinary dispatch Spanish extended ~enviar~ to letters, messengers, goods, and now email and messages (~enviar un correo~, “to send an email”). A quirk of stress splits its present tense — the accent falls on the ~i~ in ~envío~ and ~envías~ but not in ~enviamos~ — a hiatus Spanish marks with a written accent. The verb’s own nouns are ~envío~ (“shipment, dispatch”) and ~enviado~ (“envoy, correspondent”). From the same ~via~ Spanish also keeps ~vía~, ~viaje~, ~enviar~’s cousin ~desviar~ (“to divert”), ~obvio~ (“obvious,” literally “in the way”), and ~trivial~ (from ~trivium~, “a place where three roads meet”).
en.escribir:
Spanish ~escribir~ descends from Latin ~scrībere~ (“to write”), whose original sense was “to scratch, to incise.” It goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kreybʰ-~ (“to scratch, to cut”), an extension of *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut,” also behind English ~shear~). Its native cognate is Greek ~skáriphos~ (“a scratching, an outline”). Tellingly, Germanic had no inherited verb for writing and simply borrowed this one from Latin — so German ~schreiben~ and Old English ~shrive~ are early loans, not true cognates. Romance kin include Italian ~scrivere~ and French ~écrire~.

The etymology preserves the physical act: to write was to gouge marks into wax, clay or stone with a stylus long before it meant putting ink to paper. From ~scrībere~ Spanish inherited a large family: ~escritura~ (“writing; Scripture; a legal deed”), ~escritor~ (“writer”), the participle ~escrito~ (“written; a document”), and the prefixed verbs ~describir~ (“to describe”) and ~inscribir~ (“to inscribe”), plus ~manuscrito~ (“manuscript,” literally hand-written).
en.escuchar:
From Old Spanish ~ascuchar~ (also ~escuchar~), from Vulgar Latin *~ascultāre~, a metathesis of Latin ~auscultāre~ (“to listen, give ear to”). The verb was built on the stem of ~auris~ (“ear,” from *~aus-~) plus a second element from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱlew-~ (“to hear”); by another account the second piece is *~ḱel-~ (“to incline”), itself linked to *~ḱlew-~. Romance kept the word everywhere: French ~écouter~, Italian ~ascoltare~, Portuguese ~escutar~.

The sound history is memorable: Latin ~auscultāre~ shed its heavy cluster through metathesis to Vulgar Latin *~ascultāre~, and the initial ~au-~ opened to ~e-~, yielding ~escuchar~. Centuries later the medical verb ~auscultar~ (“to listen to the chest”) was borrowed afresh straight from Latin, so Spanish keeps a doublet: everyday ~escuchar~ beside learned ~auscultar~, both literally “to lend an ear.” Many speakers preserve an aspectual contrast between ~oír~ (“to hear,” passive) and ~escuchar~ (“to listen,” attentive). From the same “ear” root come ~auricular~ and, of course, ~auscultar~.
en.esperar:
From Old Spanish ~esperar~, from Latin ~spērāre~ (“to hope”), a verb built on the noun ~spēs~ (“hope”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~speh₁-~ (“to thrive, prosper”). Cognate with Italian ~sperare~, French ~espérer~, and Portuguese ~esperar~, and — through the same Latin stem — with English ~prosper~, ~desperate~, and ~despair~, this last from ~dēspērāre~ (“to lose hope”).

As with ~estar~ and ~escuela~, Spanish grew a prothetic ~e-~ before the awkward ~sp-~ cluster, turning ~spērāre~ into ~esperar~. More striking is a semantic merger unusual among the big Romance languages: ~esperar~ carries both “to hope” and “to wait, expect,” so the same verb that voices optimism also names the patience it demands — context and prepositions do the sorting, as in ~esperar a~ someone (wait) versus ~esperar que~ something happen (hope). The root flowered into ~esperanza~ (“hope”), ~espera~ (“a wait”), and the darker ~desesperar~ and ~desesperado~ (“to despair”; “desperate”), alongside ~inesperado~ (“unexpected”).
en.establecer:
From Old Spanish ~establecer~, from Latin ~stabilīre~ (“to make firm, to establish”), a verb from the adjective ~stabilis~ (“steady, firm”), from ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with French ~établir~, Italian ~stabilire~, and Portuguese ~estabelecer~; English ~establish~ was borrowed through Old French ~establir~, and its unetymological -sh reflects the Old French stressed stem.

Spanish reshaped the inherited verb with the inchoative suffix ~-ecer~ (from Latin ~-ēscere~, “to become”), the same ending seen in ~crecer~ and ~conocer~ — so ~establecer~ literally colors “to make firm” with a sense of coming-to-stand. The e- at the front is the familiar Spanish prop-vowel that Latin ~st-~ always acquires (compare ~estar~, ~escuela~). All of this rests on the great PIE root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), one of the most productive in the language: from it Spanish also has ~estable~, ~estabilidad~, ~establecimiento~, ~estado~, and ~estar~ itself.
en.estar:
From Latin ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Italic *~stāō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with Italian ~stare~ and Portuguese ~estar~, and — through the same root — with English ~stand~ and ~stay~ and French ~ester~, an Old French verb now surviving only as a legal term.

Spanish inherited two verbs from Latin's copula system and split the work of “to be” between them: ~ser~ (from ~esse~, reinforced by ~sedēre~, “to sit”) carries permanent, essential being, while ~estar~ (from ~stāre~, “to stand”) carries location, state, and condition — literally, how something “stands” at a given moment. That is why someone ~es~ tall but ~está~ tired. The past participle ~estado~ (“been; state”) gave the noun ~estado~ (“state, condition,” and by extension the political “State”). The same PIE root *~steh₂-~ seeded a vast family of Spanish words, among them ~estación~, ~estable~, ~estatua~, ~constante~, ~restar~, and ~estatuto~.
en.evitar:
Spanish ~evitar~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ēvītāre~ (“to shun, avoid”), a compound of ~ē-~/~ex-~ (“out, away”) and ~vītāre~ (“to avoid, evade”). The origin of ~vītāre~ is genuinely uncertain, and the sources disagree: by one account (De Vaan) it rests on an unattested *~vītus~ (“avoiding”), linked to Proto-Indo-European *~weyh₁-~ (“to chase, pursue”); others connect it instead to *~weyk-~ (“to yield”), or to the root of ~dīvidō~ (“to divide”). None of these is settled. Its Romance kin are straightforward: French ~éviter~, Italian ~evitare~, Portuguese ~evitar~.

Whatever its deep root, ~vītāre~ already meant in Latin “to keep clear of,” and the prefix ~ē-~ (“away”) reinforces the sense of drawing back from something — so ~evitar~ has meant “to avoid, prevent, spare” throughout its Spanish life. Because the verb entered Spanish as a learned Latinism rather than by the slow mouth-worn route of inheritance, it kept its Latin shape almost unchanged, and its Spanish family is correspondingly small and transparent: chiefly the adjectives ~evitable~ (“avoidable”) and its negation ~inevitable~ (“unavoidable”), with the adverb ~inevitablemente~. The lesson of ~evitar~ is a quieter one: not every common verb comes with a tidy prehistory, and an honest etymology sometimes ends in a shrug.
en.existir:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~exsistere~ (also ~existere~, “to step forth, emerge, come into being”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out, forth”) and ~sistere~ (“to stand, take a stand”), a reduplicated form of ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Cognate with Italian ~esistere~, French ~exister~, and Portuguese ~existir~, and — through ~sistere~ and ~stāre~ — with English ~exist~, ~insist~, ~resist~, and ~consist~, and with Spanish ~estar~.

The image hidden in ~existir~ is startlingly physical: to exist is to “stand forth,” to step out of the background into visibility. Latin ~exsistere~ first meant to emerge or come into view, and only from there did it settle into the abstract “to be.” Because it is a bookish, late-arriving word — not a battered popular inheritance — it kept its Latin shape almost intact. It supplies philosophy's most famous first person, Descartes' ~existo~ in “pienso, luego ~existo~” (“I think, therefore I am”). From it Spanish built ~existencia~ (“existence”), ~existente~, ~existencial~ and ~existencialismo~, plus ~inexistente~ (“nonexistent”) and ~coexistir~ (“to coexist”).
en.explicar:
Spanish ~explicar~ comes from Latin ~explicāre~ (“to unfold, unroll, unravel”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). ~plicāre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”). Through that root it is cognate with Greek ~plékō~ (“I plait, weave”) and German ~flechten~ (“to braid”). To explain, then, was to unfold something rolled up — to spread a folded scroll open so it could be read.

The root ~plicāre~ was extraordinarily productive. Prefixed, it gave ~aplicar~ (“to apply”), ~implicar~ (“to implicate”), ~complicar~ (“to complicate”) and ~replicar~ (“to reply”); inherited by regular sound change it became ~plegar~ (“to fold”). Its most surprising Spanish descendant is ~llegar~ (“to arrive”): from Latin ~applicāre~ (~ad-~ + ~plicāre~), which in the peninsula's seafaring usage meant to bring a ship to shore — so “to fold in to land” became simply “to arrive.” Also here: ~pliegue~ (“fold, crease”).
en.expresar:
From Late Latin ~expressāre~, a frequentative of ~exprimere~ (“to press out, squeeze out”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~premere~ (“to press”), whose past participle is ~expressus~. ~premere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~premō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~pres-~ (“to press”), an extension of *~per-~ (“to strike, press”). Cognates: French ~exprimer~, Italian ~esprimere~, English ~express~; and through ~premere~, English ~press~ and ~print~.

The metaphor is physical: ~exprimere~ meant to squeeze the juice from a fruit, and from “pressing out” juice came the figurative “pressing out” of words and feelings — to express. Spanish still holds both halves as a doublet: concrete ~exprimir~ (“to squeeze a lemon”) beside abstract ~expresar~ (“to put into words”). An ~expreso~ train, and espresso coffee, are likewise “pressed,” quick. From ~premere~ Spanish also drew ~prensa~ (“press, the press”), ~imprimir~ (“to print”), ~comprimir~, and ~oprimir~.
en.formar:
From Latin ~formāre~ (“to shape, to fashion”), from ~forma~ (“form, shape, mold”). The deeper origin of ~forma~ is genuinely disputed: one long-standing account connects it to Ancient Greek ~morphḗ~ (“shape”) by metathesis, the swapping of sounds, but scholars object that Latin shows no trace of an intermediate stage and that the required sound changes are irregular. Others reconstruct a native Proto-Indo-European source instead. Cognate with French ~former~, Italian ~formare~, and English ~form~ and ~format~.

Whatever its ultimate root, ~forma~ was one of Latin’s most productive nouns, covering shape, beauty, and pattern alike. Spanish multiplied it into ~formación~, ~fórmula~ (a diminutive, “a little form”), ~informar~ (“to give form to,” to shape into knowledge), ~transformar~, and ~uniforme~ (“of one form”). A charming survival is ~horma~, the shoemaker’s or hatmaker’s last — the wooden mold that shapes a shoe. ~horma~ is the popular, inherited descendant of ~forma~, while ~forma~ itself is the learned borrowing: a doublet in which the down-to-earth mold and the abstract idea of “form” are the same Latin word taking two roads into Spanish.
en.funcionar:
~funcionar~ is a denominal verb built on the noun ~función~, from Latin ~functiō~ (accusative ~functiōnem~), “a performing, execution,” from the deponent verb ~fungī~ (“to perform, discharge, carry out”), past participle ~functus~. This goes back to Proto-Italic *~fungōr~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰewg-~ (“to enjoy, make use of”), the present stem carrying a nasal infix. English borrowed ~function~; French has ~fonctionner~, Italian ~funzionare~.

In Latin ~fungī~ meant “to carry out a duty,” and ~función~ named the carrying-out itself; only in the modern age did Romance coin ~funcionar~ for machines and systems that “do their job” — which is why in Spanish an engine ~funciona~. A striking cousin: ~dēfungī~ meant “to finish, be done with,” so the one who has discharged life is the ~difunto~ (“deceased”), and death is a ~defunción~. From the “use up” sense comes ~fungible~ (goods consumed in use); everyday kin include the ~funcionario~, the civil servant who performs an office.
en.ganar:
The origin of ~ganar~ is debated. Corominas argues it descends, with Portuguese ~ganhar~, from a Gothic *~ganan~ (“to covet, desire eagerly”), akin to Old Norse ~gana~ (“to gape, yearn”) — a Germanic family whose primitive sense was “to open the mouth.” Its meaning was then crossed with a separate Romance family from Frankish *~waidanjan~ (“to forage, harvest, gain”): Italian ~guadagnare~, French ~gagner~ and Catalan ~guanyar~. Corominas stresses that ~ganar~ is phonetically incompatible with ~guadagnare~, so it is not simply the same word — the tidy “all from *~waidanjan~” story is exactly what he rejects.

The “desire” origin ties the verb to Spanish ~ganas~ (“urge, desire,” as in ~tener ganas~), from the very same root — a satisfying link, though it rests on the debated Gothic etymology and should be flagged as such. The senses “to gain, earn, win” all grew from there. Modern kin include ~ganancia~ (“profit”), ~ganador~ (“winner”) and, strikingly, ~ganado~ (“livestock”) — literally “what has been gained,” a reminder of an age when wealth was counted in cattle.
en.generar:
From Latin ~generāre~ (“to beget, to produce”), from ~genus~ (“birth, origin, kind”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to give birth, to beget”), one of the most fertile roots in the whole language family. Cognate with Ancient Greek ~génos~ (“race, kind”), with English ~genus~ and ~generate~, and — through Germanic — with English ~kin~ and ~kind~.

At its heart the word is about birth: to generate is to bring forth offspring, and only later, by extension, to produce anything at all — heat, electricity, income, ideas. The Latin ~genus~ meant a family or stock, which is why so much vocabulary of both kinship and classification springs from it. Spanish descendants include ~género~ (“gender, genre”), ~generación~, ~gente~ (“people,” from Latin ~gens~), ~genio~ and ~ingenio~ (the inborn talent one is “born with”), and ~degenerar~ — and, more surprisingly, ~nacer~ itself, from Latin ~nāscī~ (“to be born”), a cousin from the very same root.
en.gustar:
Spanish ~gustar~ goes back to Latin ~gustāre~ (“to taste, sample, enjoy”). Curiously, the inherited Old Spanish form was ~gostar~; modern ~gustar~ is a later reborrowing closer to the Latin, whereas Portuguese kept the inherited ~gostar~. The Latin noun ~gustus~ (“a tasting, a flavor”) comes from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵews-~ (“to taste; to choose”). Through that root ~gustar~ is cognate with English ~choose~ and with the archaic English ~gust~ (“relish, keen enjoyment”).

The remarkable Spanish development is grammatical: ~gustar~ came to mean “to be pleasing to,” so the thing tasted becomes the subject and the taster an indirect object — hence ~me gusta~ literally says “it is pleasing to me,” not “I like it.” This “to like” sense is peculiar to Ibero-Romance; the older “to taste” survives in ~degustar~ (“to taste, sample”). From the same root come ~gusto~ (“taste, pleasure”), ~gustoso~ (“tasty; glad to”) and ~disgusto~ (“displeasure, upset”).
en.haber:
Spanish ~haber~, through Old Spanish ~aver~, descends from Latin ~habēre~ (“to have, hold”), from Proto-Italic *~habēō~, and — the root is generally traced this way, though debated — from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰh₁bʰ-~ (“to grab, take, hold”). Its Romance siblings all preserve the sense of holding or possessing: French ~avoir~, Italian ~avere~, Portuguese ~haver~, and Romanian ~avea~. English ~have~ looks and sounds like an obvious cousin, but it is a false friend: it belongs to the Germanic family and, as we will see, springs from an entirely different root, so the resemblance is pure coincidence.

Where French and Italian kept ~avoir~ and ~avere~ as the everyday verb of possession, Spanish demoted ~haber~ to a near-pure auxiliary and handed ownership to ~tener~ (from Latin ~tenēre~, “to hold”). Two roles remained: the auxiliary of the compound tenses (~he cantado~, “I have sung”) and the impersonal existential ~hay~, ~había~, ~habrá~ (“there is, there are”). The old possessive sense survives only fossilized, in the noun ~haber~ / ~haberes~ (“assets, wages”) and set phrases like ~habérselas con~. The form ~hay~ deserves its own note: it is medieval ~ha~ plus the locative clitic ~y~ (from Latin ~ibī~, “there”), exactly parallel to French ~il y a~ and Catalan ~hi ha~ — literally “it has there,” hence “there is.” From the same Latin verb Spanish also draws a learned family: ~hábito~, ~habitar~, ~exhibir~, ~prohibir~, and — via ~dēbēre~, that is ~dē-~ plus ~habēre~ — the verb ~deber~.

German ~haben~ completes the trap. It comes not from the root behind ~habēre~ but from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”) — the very root that in Latin produced ~capiō~ (“I seize”), and through it Spanish ~captar~, ~cautivo~, and ~aceptar~. So the two great “have” verbs of Western Europe are not related at all; they were pulled into the same shape by a ~Sprachbund~, the long convergence of neighboring languages, until each ended up an auxiliary: Spanish ~he comido~ mirrors German ~ich habe gegessen~. There is a final twist. Old Spanish did once share the European auxiliary split, taking “be” for verbs of motion and change — ~es nacido~ (“is born”), ~so venido~ (“is come”) — but it later leveled the system, generalizing ~haber~ to every compound tense (~ha muerto~, not older ~es muerto~). So modern Spanish, unlike French and German, no longer keeps the ~ser~/~haber~ division it once had.
en.hablar:
From Old Spanish ~fablar~, from Latin ~fābulārī~ (“to chat, converse”), a verb built on ~fābula~ (“story, talk”), itself from ~fārī~ (“to speak”) and the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeh₂-~ (“to speak”). Cognate with Portuguese ~falar~ and Italian ~favellare~, and — through the same root — with Latin ~fāma~ (whence English ~fame~) and the learned English doublet ~fable~, borrowed straight from ~fābula~.

The Latin ~f~ of ~fablar~ weakened to an aspirated ~h~ in early Castilian and then fell silent, so medieval ~fablar~ became modern ~hablar~ while the letter lingered on, mute — one of the sound-changes that most sharply distinguishes Spanish from its Romance siblings. The meaning drifted too: where classical Latin used ~fābulārī~ for idle chatting, Spanish promoted it to the ordinary word for “to speak,” displacing ~loquī~. From ~fābula~ Spanish also drew the learned ~fábula~ (“fable”) and ~fabuloso~, while ~hablar~ itself seeded ~habla~ (“speech”), ~hablador~ (“chatterbox”), ~hablante~ (“speaker”), and ~hablilla~ (“rumor”).
en.hacer:
Spanish ~hacer~ comes, through Old Spanish ~fazer~, from Latin ~facere~ (“to do, to make”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, set, place”). The same root gave the English verb ~do~ and German ~tun~, so ~hacer~ and ~do~ are true cousins under the skin. Its Romance siblings kept the Latin ~f-~: Italian ~fare~, French ~faire~, Portuguese ~fazer~. Spanish alone let that ~f-~ drift to a silent ~h-~, the regular change that turned ~facere~ into ~hacer~.

Latin ~facere~ was the great all-purpose verb of doing and making, and its progeny is enormous. Spanish keeps the past participle ~hecho~ (“done; fact”), and builds ~deshacer~ (“to undo”), ~satisfacer~ (“to satisfy,” literally “to make enough”), and ~hacienda~ (“estate, treasury”). Learned borrowings that skipped the ~f-~-to-~h-~ shift preserve the older look: ~factor~, ~efecto~ (“effect”), and ~factible~ (“feasible”) — a whole workshop of words for making.
en.incluir:
A semi-learned borrowing from Latin ~inclūdere~ (“to shut in, enclose”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~claudere~ (“to close, shut”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kleh₂u-~ (“hook, peg; to close”). Cognate with Italian ~includere~, French ~inclure~, and Portuguese ~incluir~, and — through ~claudere~ — with English ~include~, ~conclude~, ~exclude~, and ~close~, plus Latin ~clāvis~ (“key,” whence Spanish ~llave~ and ~clave~).

That ~incluir~ is only semi-learned shows in its shape: a fully popular descent would have battered the word far more, but scholars and scribes reintroduced it close to the Latin, keeping the combining form ~-clūdere~ (with the ~au~ of ~claudere~ raised to ~ū~). The literal image is spatial — to shut something inside — from which the modern “to contain, comprise, include” follows directly. The same ~claudere~ radiates through Spanish ~concluir~, ~excluir~, and ~recluir~, and ~inclūdere~ itself yields ~inclusión~, the adverb ~incluso~ (“even, including”), and ~inclusivo~ (“inclusive”).
en.indicar:
From Latin ~indicāre~ (“to point out, show, declare”), from ~in-~ (“toward”) and ~dicāre~ (“to proclaim, dedicate”), a cousin of ~dīcere~ (“to say”); all go back to Proto-Indo-European *~deik-~ (“to show, point out”). It is cognate with Italian ~indicare~, Portuguese ~indicar~ and French ~indiquer~, and with English ~indicate~ and ~index~; through Germanic the same root gives English ~teach~ and ~token~.

Where ~dicāre~ was “to proclaim aloud,” ~indicāre~ was “to point a finger at,” and the finger is not incidental: the ~índice~ (“index finger”) is literally the pointer, and an ~índice~ in a book points you to its contents. From *~deik-~ Spanish gathers a wide family — ~indicio~ (“clue”), ~indicador~ (“indicator”), ~dedicar~ (“to dedicate,” from ~dēdicāre~) and ~predicar~ (“to preach,” from ~praedicāre~) — while Latin ~digitus~ (“finger”), from the same root, underlies ~dígito~ and English ~digit~.
en.informar:
From Latin ~informāre~ (“to give shape to, to form, to describe, to instruct”), a compound of ~in-~ (“into”) and ~formāre~ (“to form, to shape”), from the noun ~forma~ (“form, shape, figure”). The origin of ~forma~ is genuinely uncertain: it has long been proposed to derive from Ancient Greek ~morphḗ~ (“shape, form”) by metathesis, perhaps mediated by Etruscan, but the account is disputed and remains unproven, so the deeper source is best left open. The verb carried into Italian ~informare~, French ~informer~, and English ~inform~.

The literal sense is “to put into form,” and the abstract senses grew straight out of it: to shape the mind (“to instruct”), to shape an account (“to describe, to report”), and at last “to inform.” The very word “information” is, at root, a shaping of the mind. A charming doublet hides in the family: Spanish ~forma~ and ~horma~ (a shoemaker's “last” or mold) are the same Latin ~forma~ — one learned, one popularly inherited with ~f~ turned to ~h~. Alongside them stand ~formar~, ~fórmula~, ~formal~, ~transformar~, ~reformar~, and ~uniforme~.
en.iniciar:
From Latin ~initiāre~ (“to begin, to initiate into”), from ~initium~ (“a beginning, an entrance”), from ~inīre~ (“to go in, to enter”), which is ~in-~ (“into”) + ~īre~ (“to go”). ~īre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~eō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”), a root shared with Sanskrit ~éti~ (“he goes”) and Ancient Greek ~eîmi~ (“I will go”). Spanish borrowed the learned ~iniciar~ from Latin. Cognate with Italian ~iniziare~, French ~initier~, and Portuguese ~iniciar~.
