In Rome ~initiāre~ carried a solemn charge beyond “to begin”: it meant to admit someone into the ~initium~ — the entrance, the threshold — of the mystery religions, to initiate them into secret rites. Spanish ~iniciar~ preserves both the everyday “to start” and this ceremonial “to initiate.” The going-root *~h₁ey-~ is faint in Spanish because ~īre~ was largely replaced, but it still shows in ~ir~ (whose forms mix three Latin verbs), ~inicio~, ~iniciativa~, ~éxito~ (“a going-out,” hence “success”), and ~tránsito~.
en.intentar:
From Latin ~intentāre~ (“to stretch toward, to aim at”), a frequentative of ~intendere~ (“to direct, to focus one's attention”), formed from ~in-~ (“toward”) plus ~tendere~ (“to stretch”). ~tendere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~tendō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~tend-~, a d-extension of the root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Through that root it is cognate with Ancient Greek ~teínō~, Sanskrit ~tanóti~, and English ~thin~, ~tend~, and ~tense~. Italian ~intentare~ and Portuguese ~intentar~ preserve the same compound.

The frequentative suffix once painted a repeated, insistent stretching-toward, and from that intensified aiming the sense narrowed to “to attempt, to try.” Spanish also kept a legal and rhetorical use, where ~intentar~ una demanda means “to bring a suit.” The prolific root *~ten-~ seeded a wide family in Spanish, among them ~tender~, ~tienda~ (a “tent,” and hence a “shop”), ~tensión~, ~intención~, ~atender~, ~extender~, and ~contender~.
en.ir:
Spanish ~ir~ is, like ~ser~, a patchwork of several Latin verbs. Its infinitive and future come from Latin ~īre~ (“to go”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”), a root also visible in Greek ~eîmi~ (“I go”) and Sanskrit ~éti~. But the present tense (~voy~, ~vas~, ~va~, ~van~) comes instead from a different Latin verb, ~vādere~ (“to walk, advance”), and the preterite (~fui~, ~fue~) is borrowed wholesale from ~esse~, the perfect ~fuī~ that ~ser~ also uses.

So a single tiny verb draws on three sources — ~īre~ for the infinitive, ~vādere~ for the present, ~fuī~ for the past — one of the most thoroughly suppletive verbs in the language. The shared preterite is the memorable twist: ~fui~ means both “I went” and “I was,” the two verbs indistinguishable in that tense, context alone deciding. The ~vādere~ strand seeded further Spanish words — ~invadir~ (“to invade,” to go in), ~evadir~ (“to evade,” to go out), and ~vadear~ (“to ford”) — while ~īre~ itself left little behind but this one indispensable verb.
en.jugar:
From Latin ~iocāre~, a Vulgar-Latin variant of ~iocārī~ (“to jest, to play”), from ~iocus~ (“joke, jest”), from Proto-Indo-European *~yek-~ (“to speak”). Cognate with Italian ~giocare~, French ~jouer~, and Portuguese ~jogar~, and — through the same ~iocus~ — with English ~joke~ and ~juggle~ (the latter from Latin ~ioculārī~).

The surprise is that play began as talk. ~iocus~ was originally a spoken jest — the PIE root *~yek-~ means “to speak” — so the earliest “play” was word-play, banter, a joke. Only later did Spanish broaden ~jugar~ to cover games, sport, and gambling of every kind, leaving the verbal sense to ~bromear~. The old root still shows in ~jocoso~ (“humorous, jocular”), which kept close to the original joking. Everyday relatives include ~juego~ (“game, play”), ~jugador~ (“player”), and ~juguete~ (“toy”) — the whole vocabulary of fun grown from a single spoken quip.
en.leer:
From Latin ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick out, to choose, to read”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to collect, to gather”). Cognate with Italian ~leggere~, French ~lire~, and Portuguese ~ler~; the Greek branch, ~légō~ (“I gather, I say”), yielded ~lógos~ and the whole ~-logy~ family. Through Latin the same root gives English ~lecture~, ~legible~, ~legend~, ~collect~, and ~elect~.

The oldest sense was physical — ~legere~ meant to gather up or pick out, as one gathers firewood or picks grapes. “To read” is a metaphor grown from it: the eye gathers the scattered letters and picks out the words, one by one. Greek made the parallel leap from “gathering” to “speaking,” which is how a word for collecting became ~lógos~, “word, reason.” Spanish narrowed ~leer~ to reading alone but keeps the gathering sense in ~elegir~ (“to choose”) and ~colegir~ (“to infer, to gather”), plus the reading cluster ~lección~, ~lectura~, ~legible~, and ~leyenda~ (“legend,” literally “things to be read”).
en.llamar:
From Old Spanish ~clamar~, from Latin ~clāmāre~ (“to cry out, shout”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, shout”). Cognate with Italian ~chiamare~, French ~clamer~, and Portuguese ~chamar~, and — through the same root — with Latin ~calāre~ (“to call out”) and the English borrowings ~claim~ and ~clamor~.

The initial Latin cluster ~cl-~ palatalized to the Spanish ~ll-~ (the same shift that turned ~clāvem~ into ~llave~ and ~plēnum~ into ~lleno~), so ~clāmāre~ yielded popular ~llamar~ while a learned ~clamar~ (“to clamor, cry out”) was later re-borrowed alongside it. The sense softened from the urgency of shouting to the everyday acts of calling, summoning, and — reflexively, in ~llamarse~ — being named: one no longer cries out a name but simply ~se llama~ it. The root also gave Spanish ~clamor~, ~reclamar~ (“to claim, demand”), and ~exclamar~, plus the derivatives ~llamada~ (“call”), ~llamamiento~ (“summons”), and ~llamativo~ (“eye-catching”).
en.llegar:
From Old Spanish ~llegar~, from Latin ~plicāre~ (“to fold”) — or, by a competing account, from its compound ~applicāre~ (“to bring to, to land a ship”), the initial ~a-~ later lost. Either way the ~pl-~ hardened into Spanish ~ll-~. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”). Portuguese ~chegar~ came the same way; the folding sense stayed put in the learned doublet ~plegar~ and in Italian ~piegare~ and French ~plier~; English ~ply~ and ~apply~ are relatives.

How “to fold” became “to arrive” is debated. The usual explanation is nautical — a ship reaching harbor folds its sails, or is brought folded up against the shore — fitting for the seafaring peninsula, though it remains a proposal rather than a proven fact. Strikingly, the very same Latin verb went the opposite way in Romanian ~pleca~ (“to leave, to depart”), by one account from folding up a tent to move on — so a single root yielded both “arrive” and “leave.” Spanish derivatives include ~llegada~ (“arrival”) and the doublet family of ~plegar~, ~aplicar~, ~replicar~, and ~complicar~.
en.llevar:
From Old Spanish ~levar~, from Latin ~levāre~ (“to raise, to lift”), from the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light in weight”) — the same root that gave English its native ~light~. The Romance siblings are Italian ~levare~, French ~lever~, and Portuguese ~levar~; English also took the learned ~lever~, ~elevate~, ~alleviate~, and ~relieve~ from the same Latin stock.

The path from “to lift” to Spanish ~llevar~ (“to carry, to take, to wear”) runs through the natural chain of lifting a load, then bearing it, then bearing it away. Spanish split the work with a cousin: ~llevar~ carries something from here to there, while ~traer~ brings it toward the speaker. The plainer sense of “to raise” stayed with the doublet ~levantar~ (“to lift, to raise”), and the family also yields ~leve~ (“light, slight”), ~elevar~, ~aliviar~ (“to relieve”), ~relevar~ (“to relieve, to relay”), and ~sublevar~ (“to incite to revolt”).
en.lograr:
From Latin ~lucrārī~ (“to gain, to profit”), a deponent verb from the noun ~lucrum~ (“gain, profit, wealth”), from Proto-Indo-European *~leh₂w-~ (“to seize, to gain”). The same root surfaces in Germanic as Proto-Germanic *~launą~ (“reward”), giving German ~Lohn~ (“wage”) and Old English ~lēan~ (“reward”), and in Greek ~apolaúō~ (“to enjoy”). Within Romance, Spanish ~lograr~ stands beside the learned borrowing ~lucro~ and its Portuguese and Italian relatives.

The meaning traveled a satisfying road. Latin ~lucrārī~ was mercantile — to turn a profit — and Old Spanish ~lograr~ first meant “to enjoy or possess” something, to have the benefit of it. From “enjoying the gain” the verb slid to “obtaining the desired thing” and finally to today’s “to achieve, to manage to.” The word’s history is thus its own small success story: from raw profit, through enjoyment, to accomplishment. Alongside the popular ~lograr~ Spanish keeps the doublet ~logro~ (“achievement,” and formerly “usury, interest”), plus the learned ~lucro~ and ~lucrativo~, which stayed close to the original money-making sense.
en.mantener:
From Latin ~manū~ ~tenēre~, literally “to hold in the hand,” a phrase of ~manus~ (“hand”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold, keep”) that fused into Vulgar Latin ~manutenēre~. The second element, shared with ~tener~, goes back to Proto-Italic *~tenēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, extend”); the first, ~manus~, comes from Proto-Italic *~manus~ and *~man-~ (“hand”). Cognate Romance descendants include Italian ~mantenere~, Portuguese ~manter~ and French ~maintenir~; English ~maintain~ is the same compound, borrowed through Old French ~maintenir~.

The image is concrete: to “hold in the hand” became to keep, support, sustain and maintain — the range Spanish ~mantener~ still spans, from ~mantener~ una promesa to ~mantener~ a la familia. Its ~tenēre~ half anchors a huge family — ~tener~, ~contener~, ~detener~, ~obtener~, ~sostener~ and ~retener~ — while ~manus~ gives ~mano~, ~manejar~, ~manual~ and ~maniobra~ (“maneuver,” from ~manū~ ~operāre~, “to work by hand”). Through the root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”) ~mantener~ is even distantly kin to ~tender~, ~tienda~ (a stretched tent-shop) and English ~tenant~ and ~tension~.
en.mejorar:
Spanish ~mejorar~ comes from Late Latin ~meliōrāre~ (“to make better”), a verb built on the Latin comparative ~melior~ (“better”). ~melior~ is generally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~mel-~ (“strong, great”), the same root credited with Latin ~multus~ (“much”) and Ancient Greek ~μάλα~ (mála, “very”). Its Romance reflexes are everywhere: the adjective survives as Spanish ~mejor~, Portuguese ~melhor~, French ~meilleur~, and Italian ~migliore~, and the verb as Portuguese ~melhorar~ and Italian ~migliorare~. English ~ameliorate~ borrowed the Latin verb through French.

There is a small surprise in ~mejor~: it serves as the comparative of ~bueno~ (“good”) yet shares no root with it. Latin ~bonus~ lacked a comparative of its own and borrowed ~melior~ from an unrelated word — the pattern called suppletion, the same quirk behind English “good/better.” So ~mejorar~ means, transparently, to make or become better. From the root Spanish keeps ~mejor~, ~mejora~ (“improvement”), ~mejoría~ (“recovery”), and ~mejoramiento~; through the cognate ~multus~ come ~mucho~, ~muy~, ~multitud~, and ~múltiple~.
en.mirar:
From Latin ~mīrārī~ (“to wonder at, to marvel”), a deponent verb formed on the adjective ~mīrus~ (“wonderful, astonishing”). ~mīrus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~smeiros~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)mey-~ (“to smile, to be glad”) — so, remarkably, ~mirar~ is a blood relative of English ~smile~ and of Sanskrit ~sméra~ (“smiling”). Italian ~mirare~, French ~mirer~, and Portuguese ~mirar~ share the inheritance.

Here the surprise is a loss: Latin ~mīrārī~ was charged with astonishment, but everyday Spanish ~mirar~ drained the wonder away until it meant simply “to look at, to watch.” The amazement did not vanish, though — it took refuge in the learned offspring ~admirar~, ~milagro~ (from ~mīrāculum~), and ~maravilla~ (from ~mīrābilia~, “wonders”). English drew from the same well for ~admire~, ~miracle~, ~marvel~, and — through Vulgar Latin's “to look at” — ~mirror~, the glass you gaze into. Spanish adds ~mirada~, ~mirador~, and ~mira~.
en.morir:
From Vulgar Latin *~morīre~, a regularization of Classical Latin ~morī~ (“to die,” a deponent verb), from Proto-Indo-European *~mer-~ (“to die”). Cognate with Italian ~morire~, French ~mourir~ and Portuguese ~morrer~; through the root, with Sanskrit ~mṛtyú~ (“death”), Ancient Greek ~brotós~ (“mortal”) and — via Germanic — English ~murder~.

Classical ~morī~ was deponent (passive in form, active in meaning); Vulgar Latin recast it as an ordinary verb *~morīre~, the ancestor of every Romance form. From the participle ~mortuus~ and the noun ~mors~ (stem ~mort-~) came Spanish ~muerte~, ~muerto~, ~mortal~, ~moribundo~ and ~amortiguar~. A vivid relic survives in English ~mortgage~ — literally a “dead pledge” — while at the opposite pole Greek ~ambrosía~ (“the immortals’ food,” ~a-~ “not” + a form of *~mer-~) grows from the very same root.
en.mostrar:
From Latin ~mōnstrāre~ (“to show, point out”), a verb from the noun ~mōnstrum~ (“portent, omen, marvel”), itself derived from ~monēre~ (“to warn, remind, advise”), from Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”). Cognate with Italian ~mostrare~, French ~montrer~, and Portuguese ~mostrar~; through the same Latin family come English ~muster~ (borrowed via Old French), ~monster~, and ~demonstrate~.

The chain hides a striking image: a ~mōnstrum~ was originally a divine sign — something shown by the gods to warn mortals — so “to show” and “to warn” were once the same gesture. Latin drained the ominous charge, leaving ~mōnstrāre~ as the neutral “to point out,” while the noun kept the dread and became English ~monster~. Old Spanish ~mostrar~ inherited the plain sense of displaying and indicating. From the same root Spanish keeps ~muestra~ (“sample, sign”), ~demostrar~ (“to prove”), ~amonestar~ (“to admonish,” preserving the older warning sense), and the noun ~monstruo~, which carries the ancient shiver the verb long ago shed.
en.nacer:
From Old Spanish ~nascer~, from Vulgar Latin *~nāscere~ (a reshaping of the deponent), from Latin ~nāscī~ (“to be born”), earlier ~gnāscī~, from Proto-Italic *~gnāskōr~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget, give birth”). The initial ~gn-~ regularly simplified to ~n-~. Cognates run through Romance — Italian ~nascere~, French ~naître~, Portuguese ~nascer~ — and, through the root, Latin ~genus~ and ~gignō~ (“to beget”) and inherited English ~kin~.

The ~-sc-~ of ~nāscī~ is an inchoative suffix marking an action just beginning, so the verb frames birth as a coming-into-being in progress. From the same root *~ǵenh₁-~ Spanish drew a vast family: think of ~Navidad~, which descends from Latin ~nātīvitās~ (“birth” — the Nativity), and of ~nación~ (a people “born” together), ~naturaleza~, ~género~, and ~gente~. To be reborn is ~renacer~, the verb behind the very idea of a Renaissance.
en.necesitar:
From Latin ~necessitās~ (accusative ~necessitātem~, “necessity, unavoidability”), an abstract noun built on ~necesse~ (“necessary, inevitable”). ~necesse~ is commonly analyzed as ~ne-~ (“not”) plus ~cessus~, the past participle of ~cēdere~ (“to yield, give way”) — so its literal sense is that from which there is no yielding, though the exact formation is debated. Spanish built the verb ~necesitar~ on the inherited noun ~necesidad~ (from ~necessitātem~). It is cognate with Italian ~necessitare~, and shares its root family with French ~nécessité~, Portuguese ~necessidade~, and English ~necessity~ and ~necessary~, all drawn from the same Latin source.

In classical Latin the idea lived mostly in the impersonal phrase ~necesse est~ (“it is necessary”), so need entered Romance first as a state of affairs rather than an action; Spanish only later shaped it into a plain transitive verb. If the ~ne-~ + ~cēdere~ etymology holds, “to need” is at bottom “to have no room to give way” — necessity as a door that will not open. From the same family Spanish keeps the noun ~necesidad~, the adjective ~necesario~, and the adverb ~necesariamente~, a tidy cluster all pointing back to what cannot be avoided.
en.obtener:
Spanish ~obtener~ comes from Latin ~obtinēre~ (“to hold onto, hold fast, possess”), formed from the prefix ~ob-~ (here “toward, against”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold”). Because Spanish inherited ~tenēre~ as the everyday verb ~tener~, the compound was reshaped on that model rather than evolving purely by sound law. ~tenēre~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), which also lies, distantly, behind English ~thin~. Romance cognates include French ~obtenir~, Italian ~ottenere~ and Portuguese ~obter~.

The sense moved naturally from physically holding something to gaining and securing it — what you obtain is what you get a grip on. The root *~ten-~ (a hand stretched to hold) is one of the most productive in Spanish, giving the whole ~tener~ family: ~contener~ (“to contain”), ~mantener~ (“to maintain”), ~retener~ (“to retain”) and ~detener~ (“to stop, detain”), plus ~teniente~ (“lieutenant,” a place-holder) and the adjective ~tenaz~ (“tenacious”).
en.ocurrir:
From Latin ~occurrere~ (“to run to meet, to present itself”), an assimilated compound of ~ob-~ (“toward, to meet”) and ~currere~ (“to run”). ~currere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~korzō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). The root surfaces in English ~car~ (through Latin ~carrus~) and, by a disputed account, in English ~horse~; the verb itself continues as Italian ~occorrere~ and Portuguese ~ocorrer~.

The picture is vivid: something “runs up to meet” you, and so it “happens” or “occurs.” Spanish keeps that liveliness in the reflexive ~ocurrírsele~ algo a alguien — an idea literally runs up to a person's mind, that is, “it occurs to them.” The event sense and the mental sense have coexisted since Latin. The running-root spread widely in Spanish: ~correr~, ~corriente~, ~carrera~, ~recorrer~, ~concurrir~, ~discurrir~, ~socorrer~, and the school word ~currículo~ (from ~currículum~, “a course, a running”).
en.ofrecer:
From Old Spanish ~ofrecer~ (also ~ofrir~), from a Vulgar Latin inchoative *~offerēscere~ reshaping Latin ~offerre~ (“to present, offer”), a compound of ~ob-~ (“toward, before”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰer-~ (“to bear, carry”). Cognate with Italian ~offrire~, French ~offrir~, and Portuguese ~oferecer~, and — through ~ferre~ and its root — with English ~bear~ and the Latin borrowings ~offer~ and ~transfer~.

The extra syllable in ~ofrecer~ comes from the Latin inchoative suffix ~-ēscere~, which marked the beginning of an action and pulled the verb into the large Spanish ~-ecer~ class alongside ~parecer~, ~crecer~, and ~conocer~. Semantically the word kept ~offerre~'s literal image of “carrying something before” another — to present a gift, a price, resistance, or oneself. Its religious weight survives in ~ofrenda~ (“offering, oblation”) and the participle-noun ~oferta~ (“offer, bargain”), while the shared root ~ferre~ radiates through ~conferir~, ~preferir~, ~referir~, and ~transferir~, and ~ofrecer~ itself yields ~ofrecimiento~ (“offer, offering”).
en.organizar:
From Medieval Latin ~organizāre~ (“to furnish with organs, to arrange into a working whole”), from Latin ~organum~ (“instrument, tool, organ”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~órganon~ (ὄργανον, “tool, instrument”). ~órganon~ derives from ~érgon~ (“work, deed”) and the Proto-Indo-European *~werǵ-~ (“to do, to work”). That root is shared, remarkably, with English ~work~ and German ~Werk~. Spanish took ~organizar~ through learned channels. Cognate with Italian ~organizzare~ and French ~organiser~.

The chain of sense is elegant: an ~órganon~ was a tool for doing work, then a bodily “instrument” (an organ), and a body is many organs cooperating — so to ~organizar~ is to make separate parts function together like the organs of a living whole. The word lived in Spanish first in that biological and musical sense (the ~órgano~, the church instrument of many pipes) before it broadened to committees and revolutions. From the same *~werǵ-~ come ~órgano~, ~organismo~, ~orgía~ (Greek rites, literally “workings”), ~cirugía~ (“hand-work”), and ~energía~.
en.pagar:
Spanish ~pagar~ comes from Late Latin ~pācāre~ (“to pacify, appease, satisfy”), a verb on ~pāx~ (“peace”). ~pāx~ goes back, through Proto-Italic *~pāks~, to Proto-Indo-European *~peh₂ḱ-~ (“to fasten, join”) — peace conceived as the binding-together of parties — a root shared with Latin ~pangere~ (“to fix, fasten”) and ~pacīscī~ (“to make a pact”). Its Romance reflexes include French ~payer~, Portuguese ~pagar~, Italian ~pagare~, and Catalan ~pagar~; English ~pay~ was borrowed from Old French ~paiier~.

The meaning traveled a very human road: to ~pācāre~ a creditor was to “appease” him, and appeasing a creditor means handing over money — so “pacify” slid into “pay.” The old sense still peeks through: someone ~pagado de sí mismo~ is “pleased with himself,” satisfied rather than paid. From ~pāx~ Spanish gathered ~paz~ (“peace”), ~pago~ (“payment”), ~pagador~, ~pacífico~, ~pacto~, and ~apaciguar~ (“to appease”). Most striking is ~apagar~ (“to switch off, extinguish”), from Vulgar Latin *~appācāre~: to quiet a flame is, quite literally, to make peace with it.
en.parecer:
From Old Spanish ~pareçer~, from Vulgar Latin *~parēscere~, an inchoative formed on Latin ~pārēre~ (“to appear, become visible, show oneself”). The inchoative suffix ~-ēscere~ marked a coming-into-view, which the ~-ecer~ ending of Spanish still carries. Cognate with Italian ~parere~, French ~paraître~, Portuguese ~parecer~, and Catalan ~parèixer~; through Latin ~appārēre~ English is kin by way of ~appear~ and ~apparent~.

Latin ~pārēre~ meant “to come into sight”; the inchoative *~parēscere~ stressed the moment of appearing, and from “to appear” Spanish ~parecer~ slid naturally into “to seem” — for what appears is not always what is. Reflexive ~parecerse~ took the further step to “to resemble,” and the noun use in ~el parecer~ means an “opinion,” literally how a thing appears to someone. The prefixed ~aparecer~ (“to appear”) and ~desaparecer~ (“to disappear”) stayed closer to the root sense, while ~comparecer~ (“to appear in court”) narrowed it to legal presence. From the same base come ~aparición~, ~apariencia~, ~parecido~, and ~aparente~.
en.participar:
From Latin ~participāre~ (“to share, to partake”), from the adjective ~particeps~ (“sharing, partaking”), a compound of ~pars~ (“part”) and ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”) — literally “taking a part.” ~capere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). Cognate with French ~participer~, Italian ~partecipare~, and English ~participate~ and ~participle~.

The image behind the word is delightfully literal: to participate is to take your portion of something shared. Latin ~particeps~ was originally an everyday adjective for anyone who had a share in an affair. From ~pars~ Spanish drew a large family — ~parte~, ~partícipe~, ~participio~ (the grammatical “participle,” which likewise “shares” properties of verb and adjective), and ~partido~ (“party, match”). The other half, ~capere~, is even more prolific, giving ~caber~ (“to fit”), ~captar~, and even ~cazar~ (“to hunt,” i.e., to catch). To take part, in short, is to seize your slice.
en.partir:
Spanish ~partir~ descends from Latin ~partīre~ (also deponent ~partīrī~, “to divide, to share out”), a verb built on the noun ~pars~ (stem ~partis~, “a part, a share”). The deeper prehistory of ~pars~ is debated: it is usually linked with Latin ~pār~ (“equal”), ~portiō~ (“portion”) and ~parāre~ (“to make ready”), but the Proto-Indo-European root behind them is disputed and no single reconstruction is secure. Romance cognates are plentiful — French ~partir~, Italian ~partire~, Portuguese ~partir~ — and English ~part~ was borrowed from the same Latin stock.

~partir~ still means both “to split” and “to share,” but it also took on the sense “to depart” — to part from company, to set out (~partir de viaje~, “to leave on a trip”); French carried that branch all the way, so its ~partir~ means simply “to leave.” The noun ~pars~ underlies a broad Spanish family: ~parte~ (“part”), ~partido~ (“party; match”), ~partícula~ (“particle”), ~repartir~ (“to distribute”), ~compartir~ (“to share”) and the musical ~partitura~ (“score”).
en.pasar:
From Late Latin ~passāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~passus~ (“a step, a pace”), originally the past participle of ~pandere~ (“to spread out, to stretch”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to spread”). Cognate with Italian ~passare~, French ~passer~, and Portuguese ~passar~; English ~pass~ entered through Old French rather than directly from Latin.

The image at the root is bodily: a ~passus~ was the stretch of the legs in a single stride, and by extension the Roman unit of distance measured by that stride. From “to take a step” the verb widened to “to move past, to cross, to go through,” and then to the whole sweep of senses Spanish now gives it — to happen (« ¿qué pasa? »), to spend time, to pass an exam, to hand something over. The same family seeded ~paso~ (“step”), ~pasaje~ (“passage, fare”), ~pasaporte~ (literally a warrant to ~pasar~ a port or gate), ~paseo~ (“a stroll”), and the ubiquitous ~pasado~ (“the past; passed”).
en.pedir:
From Latin ~petere~ (“to make for, to seek, to ask, to aim at, even to attack”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to fly, to rush”). The root’s flight-sense shows plainly in its cognates: Greek ~pétomai~ (“I fly”) and ~píptō~ (“I fall”), Sanskrit ~pátati~ (“flies, falls”), and — through Germanic — English ~feather~, literally “the flying thing.” In Romance, Portuguese ~pedir~ is the direct sibling; Italian and French chose other verbs for “to ask.”

The semantic heart is motion toward a target: ~petere~ first meant to rush at or make for something, which is why the one verb could mean both “to attack” and “to request” — to ask is to launch yourself at what you want. Spanish wore the sound down to the humble ~pedir~, but the vigorous original survives in a crowd of learned relatives: ~petición~ (“petition, request”), ~competir~ (“to compete,” to seek alongside), ~apetito~ (“appetite,” a seeking-toward), ~ímpetu~ (“impetus, a rushing upon”), ~repetir~ (“to seek again”), and ~perpetuo~ (“continually rushing onward”). English shares the set through ~petition~, ~compete~, ~appetite~, and ~impetus~.
en.pensar:
From Old Spanish ~pensar~, from Latin ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh, ponder”), the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to hang”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, stretch”). Cognate with Italian ~pensare~, French ~penser~, and Portuguese ~pensar~, and — through the same stem — with English ~pensive~, ~ponder~, and ~pension~; Spanish keeps a doublet in ~pesar~ (“to weigh; to grieve”).

The heart of this word is a metaphor so old it feels literal: to think is to weigh one thing against another. Latin ~pēnsāre~ meant to weigh out repeatedly, hence to ponder, to balance one option against the next — and Spanish ~pensar~ still does exactly that. The same ~pēnsāre~ took a different turn in French ~panser~ (“to dress a wound, tend a horse”), from the sense “to attend to,” a nice reminder of how far one root can wander. From it Spanish drew ~pensamiento~ (“thought”), ~pensador~ (“thinker”), ~pensativo~ (“pensive”), and ~pensión~ (“pension”), while the popular doublet ~pesar~ gave the noun ~peso~ (“weight; the currency”).
en.perder:
From Latin ~perdere~ (“to lose, to ruin, to squander”), a compound of the prefix ~per-~ (here “thoroughly, to destruction”) and an element ~-dere~. That second element is traditionally identified with ~dare~ (“to give,” from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~), which would make ~perdere~ a “giving away through and through”; but many etymologists now trace the ~-dere~ of such compounds instead to PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to place”), and the point remains debated. Either way the Romance descent is uniform: Italian ~perdere~, French ~perdre~, Portuguese ~perder~, and Romanian ~pierde~.

Whatever the deep root, the Latin sense was strong — not mild misplacement but thorough undoing: ~perdere~ could mean to destroy, to bring to ruin, as well as to lose. Spanish softened it to everyday “losing,” yet the darker charge survives in ~perdición~ (“perdition, ruin”) and in phrases like ~echar a perder~ (“to spoil, to wreck”). If the older ~dare~ analysis is right, to lose is to “give something away completely,” an oddly generous image for misfortune; if the *~dʰeh₁-~ analysis is right, it is rather to “put something clean out of reach.” From the verb Spanish keeps ~pérdida~ (“loss”), ~perdido~ (“lost”), and ~perdición~.
en.permitir:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~permittere~ (“to let through, give up, allow”), from ~per-~ (“through”) plus ~mittere~ (“to send, let go, release”); ~mittere~ is of uncertain further origin, with no secure Proto-Indo-European etymology. Cognate with Italian ~permettere~, French ~permettre~, and Portuguese ~permitir~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~permit~. The base ~mittere~ underlies a huge Romance and English family.

In Latin ~mittere~ first meant “to send,” and ~permittere~ literally “to send through” — to let something pass — from which grew the idea of granting passage, yielding, and finally “allowing.” Because Spanish took ~permitir~ from written Latin rather than through gradual sound-change, it kept the Latin shape almost intact, unlike its inherited cousin ~meter~ (“to put in”), which descends from the very same ~mittere~ by the popular route. That double inheritance — learned and popular — makes ~mittere~ one of the most productive Latin verbs in Spanish: ~permiso~, ~mensaje~ and ~mensajero~ (from ~missus~), ~misión~, ~remitir~, ~admitir~, ~cometer~, ~prometer~, ~someter~, and ~transmitir~ all spring from it.
en.pesar:
From Latin ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh carefully”), the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to hang, to weigh, to pay”), from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)pen-~ (“to draw, stretch, spin”). Cognate with French ~peser~, Italian ~pesare~, and Portuguese ~pesar~, and — through the same root — with English ~pension~ and ~pendant~, both of which recall the old link between weighing and paying.

Roman merchants weighed coins to check their value, and ~pēnsāre~ carried that sense of careful assessment. Spanish inherited the verb twice: the popular line gave ~pesar~ (“to weigh”), while a more learned development gave ~pensar~ (“to think”) — literally, to weigh ideas in the mind. The two are doublets, one physical and one mental. ~pesar~ also came to name sorrow (~a pesar de~, “in spite of”; the noun ~pesar~, “grief”), as though sadness were a weight pressing down. The same family yielded ~peso~ (“weight,” and the currency), ~pesado~ (“heavy”), ~compensar~, and ~dispensar~.
en.poder:
Spanish ~poder~ descends from a Vulgar Latin verb *~potēre~, a regularized reshaping of Classical Latin ~posse~ (“to be able”). ~posse~ was itself a contraction of ~potis~ (“able, powerful”) plus ~esse~ (“to be”) — “to be able” quite literally “to be capable.” The Proto-Indo-European root is *~poti-~ (“powerful, master”). The reshaped infinitive spread across Romance: Italian ~potere~, French ~pouvoir~, and Portuguese ~poder~.

Like several verbs of ability, ~poder~ doubles as a noun — ~el poder~, “power” itself, the thing one has the capacity to wield. The root's sense of capability and dominance fans out across the vocabulary: ~poderoso~ (“powerful”), ~poderío~ (“might”), ~potente~ and ~potencia~ (“potent,” “power”), ~posible~ (“possible,” what one is able to do), and ~potestad~ (“authority”). Even the English ~potent~ and ~possible~ belong to the same family, borrowed from the same Latin stock.
en.poner:
From Latin ~pōnere~ (“to put, to place, to set down”), earlier *~posinere~, analyzed as the prefix ~po-~ (“away, off”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, to leave”) — so to “put” was first to “set aside, to let stand.” From Proto-Italic *~posinō~. Its Romance offspring include Portuguese ~pôr~, Italian ~porre~, and French ~pondre~, which narrowed touchingly to mean “to lay eggs.” English holds the root through the learned forms ~position~, ~component~, ~deposit~, and ~compound~.

Because a bird “puts” its eggs in the nest, French preserved the most literal descendant of all; Spanish keeps that sense too in ~poner un huevo~ (“to lay an egg”), alongside every other kind of placing. ~poner~ is also famously irregular — its past participle is ~puesto~, its preterite ~puse~ — and it swarms with prefixes: ~componer~ (“to compose”), ~disponer~ (“to arrange”), ~proponer~ (“to propose”), ~suponer~ (“to suppose”), and ~exponer~ (“to expose”). From the participle ~puesto~ come the nouns ~posición~, ~postura~, and ~puesto~ (“post, stall, position”).
en.preguntar:
Spanish ~preguntar~ comes from a Vulgar Latin *~praecontāre~ (or *~praecunctāre~), a reshaping of Classical Latin ~percontārī~ (“to question, inquire”). ~percontārī~ was built from ~per-~ (“through”) and, by the traditional account, ~contus~ (“a long pole,” borrowed from Greek ~kontós~): it was originally a sailors’ word meaning to sound the depth of water with a pole — and, by an old and vivid metaphor, to probe or sound out a person with questions. In Vulgar Latin the prefix ~per-~ was refashioned as ~prae-~ (~pre-~), perhaps under the influence of ~cunctārī~ (“to hesitate, delay”). Portuguese ~perguntar~ keeps the original ~per-~; Spanish generalized ~pre-~.

The pole is the memorable image, but it should be flagged: the derivation of ~percontārī~ from ~contus~ (“pole”) is the traditional explanation and is plausible, yet not beyond dispute, so the seafaring picture is best offered as the received story rather than proven fact. What is certain is that the sense narrowed cleanly to “to ask,” and that Spanish generalized the ~pre-~ form across the board. From it come the noun ~pregunta~ (“question”), ~preguntón~ (“inquisitive; a busybody”), and the reflexive ~preguntarse~ (“to wonder, ask oneself”). A useful pair to keep straight: ~preguntar~ is “to ask a question,” while ~pedir~ (from Latin ~petere~) is “to ask for, request” — Spanish, unlike English, never lets one verb do both jobs.
en.preparar:
From Latin ~praeparāre~ (“to make ready beforehand”), from ~prae-~ (“before”) + ~parāre~ (“to make ready, provide”), from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to provide, grant”). Cognate with Italian ~preparare~, French ~préparer~, Portuguese ~preparar~ and English ~prepare~; through the root, with Latin ~parere~ (“to give birth, bring forth”) and Sanskrit ~pṛṇā́ti~ (“to grant, bestow”).

The simple verb ~parāre~ meant “to make ready,” and its offspring fanned out across Spanish: ~parar~ (“to stop”), ~preparación~, ~preparativo~, ~aparato~ (“apparatus”), ~reparar~, ~separar~ and ~amparar~ (“to shelter”). Through the closely related ~parere~ (“to bear young”) come ~parir~ and ~parto~ (“childbirth”). The root’s basic idea is provision: to prepare is to have things furnished in advance, ready to hand.
en.presentar:
From Latin ~praesentāre~ (“to place before, show, offer”), the verb of ~praesēns~ (“present, at hand”), the present participle of ~praeesse~ (“to be before, be at hand”), from ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) plus ~esse~ (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁es-~ (“to be”). Cognate with Italian ~presentare~, French ~présenter~, Portuguese ~apresentar~, and English ~present~ and ~represent~.

The core image is spatial: ~prae-~ “before” plus ~esse~ “to be,” so ~praesēns~ described whatever “is before you,” present in place and in time. From ~praesentāre~, “to set before someone,” Spanish ~presentar~ branched into introducing a person, showing a document, staging a show, and lodging a complaint — every sense a variation on putting something in front of an audience. The adjective and noun ~presente~ carries both meanings the Latin fused: the present moment and a present, a gift “placed before” the receiver. From the same ~prae-~ + ~esse~ come ~presencia~, ~presentación~, ~presentador~, and ~presentimiento~ (“foreboding,” a feeling that “is there beforehand”).
en.privar:
From Latin ~prīvāre~ (“to deprive, to strip of, to free from”), a verb built on the adjective ~prīvus~ (“single, one's own, set apart”). ~prīvus~ traces to Proto-Italic *~preiwos~ and is generally linked to the Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“forward, in front”), by a semantic shift from “standing in front” to “standing apart, being separate.” The Romance descendants are learned rather than inherited: Italian ~privare~, French ~priver~, Portuguese ~privar~. English ~private~ and ~deprive~ belong to the same Latin family.

~prīvus~ first meant “single, individual” — one thing set apart from the common stock — so ~prīvāre~ was to set apart, and thus to take away, to deprive. The same “set apart for oneself” idea runs the other way in ~prīvātus~, what is withdrawn from public life into the private sphere; a Roman ~prīvātus~ was a citizen holding no public office. From ~prīvus~ Spanish gathered ~privado~ (“private”), ~privación~, ~privilegio~ (“a law for one person,” ~prīvus~ + ~lex~), and the adjective ~privativo~. Curiously, ~privar~ also came to mean “to be in favor” or, colloquially, “to be all the rage.”
en.producir:
Spanish ~producir~ descends from Latin ~prōdūcere~ (“to lead forth, bring forth, produce”), a compound of the prefix ~prō-~ (“forward”) and the verb ~dūcere~ (“to lead, draw”). ~dūcere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to lead, draw”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~tow~ and German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”); the Latin verb itself, inherited across Romance, gave Italian ~produrre~ and French ~produire~, and — borrowed — English ~produce~.

Latin ~prōdūcere~ literally meant to lead something forward into view, and from that concrete image the abstract senses of causing, generating and manufacturing developed. The same ~dūcere~ seeded a large Spanish family in ~-ducir~: ~conducir~ (“to drive, conduct”), ~traducir~ (“to translate,” literally to lead across) and ~reducir~ (“to reduce, lead back”), alongside the nouns ~ducto~ and ~duque~ (“the one who leads”). Its participle ~producto~ gave the everyday noun for a “product.”
en.proponer:
From Latin ~prōpōnere~ (“to set forth, put forward”), from ~prō-~ (“forward”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, place”). By the standard analysis ~pōnere~ is itself ~po-~ + ~sinere~ (“to let, set down”), from Proto-Italic *~pozinō~, with the prefix going back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂epó~ (“off, away”) — though this decomposition is a reconstruction, not an attested split. Italian inherits the compound directly as ~proporre~, Portuguese as ~propor~. French ~proposer~ and English ~propose~, however, belong to the ~poser~ family (from Late Latin ~pausāre~, “to pause, rest”), which merged in sense with the ~pōnere~ compounds — a famous etymological tangle.

The core sense is spatial: ~prōpōnere~ is to put a thing forward, to set it before others — before the eyes as an offer, before the mind as a proposition. Latin's participle ~prōpositum~ gave Spanish ~propósito~ (“purpose, what one sets before oneself as a goal”) and ~proposición~, while the deverbal noun is ~propuesta~ (“a proposal”). Few Latin stems were as fertile as ~pōnere~: from it Spanish built ~poner~ and a whole rank of compounds — ~componer~, ~disponer~, ~oponer~, ~suponer~ — each “placing” in its own direction.
en.publicar:
From Latin ~publicāre~ (“to make public, publish”), from ~pūblicus~ (“public, of the people”), an alteration of Old Latin ~poplicus~, from ~populus~ (“the people,” itself of unknown origin). The shift of ~poplicus~ to ~pūblicus~ — the ū and the b — is usually credited to the pull of ~pūbēs~ (“adult population”), though whether this is true blending or mere association is debated. It is cognate with Italian ~pubblicare~, Portuguese ~publicar~ and French ~publier~, and — through that French — with English ~publish~.

Latin ~publicāre~ meant to make something common property, even “to confiscate for the state,” and more broadly “to make known.” Only with the printing press did “make known” specialize into “issue a book,” the sense Spanish ~publicar~ now carries first. From the same ~populus~ Spanish drew a broad family: ~público~ (“public”), ~publicidad~ (“advertising, publicity”), ~popular~, ~pueblo~ (“people, town”) and, from ~rēs pūblica~ (“the public thing”), ~república~.
en.quedar:
From Latin ~quiētāre~ (“to calm, quiet, bring to rest”), the verb of ~quiētus~ (“at rest, calm, quiet”), the past participle of ~quiēscere~ (“to rest”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kʷyeh₁-~ (“to rest, be at peace”). Cognate with Italian ~quietare~ and Old Portuguese ~quedar~; through ~quiētus~ Spanish is kin to English ~quiet~, ~quit~, ~coy~ (via French ~coi~), and the noun ~quietus~, and — through the same root — to English ~while~.

The semantic heart of ~quedar~ is stillness: to ~quedar~ somewhere is, at root, to “come to rest” there, and from “grow calm” the verb widened into “remain, stay, be left over,” and reflexively ~quedarse~ (“to stay put”). Spanish also turned it into everyday idiom — ~quedar en~ (“to agree on”), ~quedar bien~ (“to make a good impression”), and ~quedar con~ (“to arrange to meet”) — senses far from the original hush. The same root left the adjective ~quieto~ (“still”), the nouns ~quietud~ and ~inquietud~ (“restlessness, unease”), and the verb ~aquietar~ (“to soothe”); the archaic adverb ~quedo~ (“softly, quietly”) preserves the ancestor most faithfully.
en.querer:
From Latin ~quaerere~ (“to seek, to ask for, to strive after”), inherited through Old Spanish ~querer~. The verb’s deeper ancestry is uncertain: by one proposal it reflects Proto-Indo-European *~kʷeh₂-~ (“to acquire”), with cognates such as Ancient Greek ~pépamai~ (“to acquire”); other scholars connect it instead to a root meaning “to seek, to ask,” and the question remains unsettled. Its Romance kin include Portuguese ~querer~ and Old French ~quérir~.

Where Latin ~quaerere~ meant to search or to petition, Spanish let the sense drift inward — from “to seek” to “to want,” and at last to “to love,” which is why ~te quiero~ — literally “I want you” — is the everyday way to say “I love you.” The learned branch of the family kept the older, more forensic flavor: ~cuestión~ (“question, matter”), ~encuesta~ (“survey”), ~pesquisa~ (“inquiry”), ~requerir~, ~adquirir~, ~inquirir~, ~conquistar~, and ~querella~ (“legal complaint”) all descend from ~quaerere~. English shares the harvest through ~query~, ~quest~, ~question~, ~require~, and ~conquer~.
en.realizar:
A comparatively young verb: Spanish ~realizar~ was formed from the adjective ~real~ (“real, actual”) with the suffix ~-izar~, on the model of Medieval Latin ~reālizāre~ and French ~réaliser~. ~real~ goes back to Late Latin ~reālis~ (“relating to things”), from Latin ~rēs~ (“thing, matter, affair”), from Proto-Indo-European *~reh₁ís~ (“wealth, goods”), akin to Sanskrit ~rayí~ (“property, riches”). English ~real~ and ~realize~ share the same source.

So the verb’s hidden sense is “to make into a thing” — to turn what was only planned or imagined into something that exists. That gives Spanish two everyday meanings that English splits apart: ~realizar~ is both “to carry out, to accomplish” (« realizar un proyecto ») and, more recently and under English influence, “to realize, to become aware.” From the same ~rēs~ descend ~real~, ~realidad~ (“reality”), ~realismo~, the legal ~res~ still used in Latin tags, and — through ~rēs pūblica~ (“the public thing”) — the word ~república~.
en.recibir:
From Old Spanish ~recebir~, from Latin ~recipere~ (“to take back, receive, accept”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~capere~ (“to take, seize”). This ~capere~ traces to Proto-Italic *~kapjō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~kap-~ (“to grasp, seize”), the same root that gave, through Germanic, English ~have~ and ~heave~. Cognate with Portuguese ~receber~, Italian ~ricevere~ and French ~recevoir~; English ~receive~ descends from the same Latin verb by way of Old French.

Latin ~recipere~ literally meant to take something back to oneself, and from that grew the senses of accepting, admitting and welcoming that Spanish ~recibir~ still carries. Its past participle ~recepta~ (“things received”) gave ~receta~, which in Spanish names both a cooking recipe and a doctor’s prescription — each a little list of things to be taken. The root ~capere~ seeded a broad family: ~recepción~, ~recibo~, ~captura~, ~cautivo~, ~capaz~, ~concebir~ and ~percibir~ all turn on the idea of taking hold.
en.reconocer:
Spanish ~reconocer~ descends from Latin ~recognōscere~ (“to recall, recognize”), a compound of ~re-~ (“again”) and ~cognōscere~ (“to become acquainted with, learn”), itself ~con-~ (an intensifying “thoroughly”) plus ~gnōscere~ (“to come to know”). Through Proto-Italic *~gnōskō~ the verb reaches Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know, recognize”). That root is among the most widely attested in the family, cognate with English ~know~, Ancient Greek ~γιγνώσκω~ (gignṓskō, “to know”), and Latin ~nōtus~ (“known”). French ~reconnaître~ and Italian ~riconoscere~ are its Romance siblings.

The compound is transparent: to ~reconocer~ is quite literally to “know again,” the ~re-~ marking a second, confirming encounter with what one already knew. From that core Spanish stretched the verb across many fields — acknowledging a debt, scouting ground (~reconocer el terreno~), a doctor’s checkup (~reconocimiento médico~). The same PIE root seeded a wide family: the plain ~conocer~ (“to know”), ~conocimiento~ (“knowledge”), ~noción~, ~noticia~ (“news”), and ~noble~, alongside the negated ~ignorar~ (“to not know”) and ~incógnito~. By way of Greek the root also yielded ~diagnóstico~. Few etymologies link a Spanish everyday word to English ~know~ so plainly across five millennia.
en.recordar:
Spanish ~recordar~ comes from Latin ~recordārī~ (“to remember, to call to mind”), from the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~cor~ (stem ~cordis~, “heart”) — so to remember was, literally, to bring something back through the heart. ~cor~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~ḱerd-~ (“heart”), the native cognate of English ~heart~ and German ~Herz~. English ~record~ is the very same Latin verb, borrowed through French — a doublet of ~recordar~.

The etymology encodes an old idea: the ancients seated memory and thought not in the brain but in the heart, so recalling was a movement of the heart. That is why “to record” and “to remember” share one word. From ~cor~ Spanish inherited ~corazón~ (“heart”) and built a wide family: ~acordar~ (“to agree; to remind”), the noun ~recuerdo~ (“a memory, a souvenir”), ~cordial~ (“heartfelt”), ~concordia~ (“concord, a harmony of hearts”) and its opposite ~discordia~ (“discord”).
en.reducir:
Spanish ~reducir~ comes from Latin ~redūcere~ (“to lead back, bring back”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~dūcere~ (“to lead, draw, guide”). ~dūcere~ reflects Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to lead, draw”), a root remarkably productive in both branches: in Germanic it gave English ~tow~ and ~tug~, plus the borrowed ~duke~ (via Latin ~dux~, “leader”), and German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”) and ~Zug~ (“train, pull”). Latin ~dūcere~ alone spun off ~condūcere~, ~prōdūcere~, ~indūcere~ and dozens more. Italian ~ridurre~, French ~réduire~, and Portuguese ~reduzir~ are the Romance siblings of ~reducir~.

The core sense was spatial — to ~redūcere~ was to lead something back to where it came from. From “bring back” Latin developed “bring to a state or condition,” and that is the sense Spanish generalized: to reduce is to bring a thing back or down to something smaller, simpler, or more basic. Hence ~reducir~ spans lowering a price, boiling down a sauce (~reducir una salsa~), subduing an enemy (~reducir al enemigo~), and setting a broken bone (~reducir una fractura~ — literally leading it back into place). From the same ~dūcere~ root Spanish holds ~conducir~, ~producir~, ~educar~, ~duque~, ~ducha~ (“shower,” via Italian ~doccia~), and ~acueducto~.
en.referir:
Directly from Latin ~referre~ (“to carry back, to bring back word, to report”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”). ~ferre~ traces to Proto-Italic *~ferō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”), the same immensely productive root that gives Ancient Greek ~phérō~, Sanskrit ~bhárati~, and English ~bear~. The verb lives on in Italian ~riferire~, French ~référer~, and Portuguese ~referir~.

The core image is concrete — to carry something back to a source or a listener — which is why ~referir~ spans “to recount,” “to report,” and, reflexively as ~referirse~, “to allude to.” A fossil of Roman grammar rides along in ~referéndum~: it is a gerundive, literally “matters that must be carried back” to the people for a vote. English borrowed the same stem for ~referee~ and ~reference~. Within Spanish the compound sits beside its siblings ~conferir~, ~inferir~, ~proferir~, and ~transferir~, and beside the noun family ~referencia~ and ~relación~.
en.relacionar:
A modern denominal verb: Spanish ~relación~ (“relation”) plus the verb-forming ~-ar~. ~relación~ comes from Latin ~relātiōnem~ (accusative of ~relātiō~, “a carrying back, a report”), built on ~relātus~, the participle of ~referre~ (“to carry back, to report”), from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”). ~ferre~ rests on Proto-Italic *~ferō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”) — one of the most widespread of all roots, cognate with Ancient Greek ~phérō~, Sanskrit ~bhárati~, and English ~bear~. Portuguese matches it as ~relacionar~.

Notably, where English took ~relate~ straight from the Latin participle, Spanish assembled ~relacionar~ later and from the noun, so it literally means “to put into relation.” A quirk of ~ferre~ is that its own past participle ~lātus~ is suppletive, borrowed from an unrelated root — which is why the “-lation” words look nothing like “fer-.” The vast *~bʰer-~ family in Spanish includes ~referir~, ~preferir~, ~transferir~, ~conferir~, ~diferir~, and — through ~offerre~ and ~sufferre~ — ~ofrecer~ and ~sufrir~.
en.representar:
From Latin ~repraesentāre~ (“to make present, to bring before one, to display”), from ~re-~ + ~praesentāre~ (“to present”), from the adjective ~praesens~ (“present, at hand”). ~praesens~ is itself ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) plus a participle of ~esse~ (“to be”) — literally, “being before” one's eyes. Spanish took the learned ~representar~ from Latin, alongside the noun ~representación~. Cognate with Italian ~rappresentare~, French ~représenter~, Portuguese ~representar~, and, through Old French, English ~represent~.

The core image is theatrical and literal at once: to ~representar~ is to make something ~praesens~ — present again, brought back before the eyes — whether a lawyer standing in for a client, an actor embodying a role, or a sign standing for a thing. Latin ~repraesentāre~ also meant “to pay on the spot, in cash,” the immediacy of ready money. From ~praesens~ and ~esse~ Spanish gathered ~presente~, ~presencia~, ~representante~, and ~ausente~ (“absent,” from ~ab-~ + the same participle), the mirror image of being there.
en.requerir:
From Latin ~requīrere~ (“to seek again, to ask for, to need”), from ~re-~ (“again, back”) + ~quaerere~ (“to seek, to ask”). The Old Spanish form was ~requerir~, remodeled on the many ~-quirere~ compounds. The origin of ~quaerere~ itself is uncertain: it is usually traced to Proto-Italic *~kʷaizō~ and a Proto-Indo-European *~kʷeh₂-~ (“to acquire”), though older proposals connected it instead to roots meaning “to seek” or “to see.” Cognate compounds gave English ~require~, ~acquire~, and ~inquire~, and the base survives in Spanish ~querer~ and French ~quérir~.

~quaerere~ meant “to seek,” and its ~re-~ intensified that into “to seek insistently, to demand” — the sense modern ~requerir~ keeps when a law or a task “requires” something of us. The plain verb took a startling turn on Spanish soil: it became ~querer~, “to want, to love,” so the Latin idea of seeking softened into Spanish desiring. From the same family come ~cuestión~ (“question”), ~pesquisa~ (“inquiry”), ~encuesta~ (“survey”), ~adquirir~, and ~conquistar~.
en.responder:
From Latin ~respondēre~ (“to answer; to promise in return”), from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~spondēre~ (“to pledge, promise solemnly”), from Proto-Italic *~spondeō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~spend-~ (“to make an offering, perform a rite”). Cognates fill Romance — Italian ~rispondere~, French ~répondre~, Portuguese ~responder~ — and reach English ~respond~; Ancient Greek ~σπένδω~ (“to pour a libation”) shares the root, as, through the participle, does English ~spouse~.

The buried image is ritual: ~spondēre~ was to make a solemn pledge, first sworn over a libation poured to the gods — exactly the sense of Greek ~σπένδω~ — so to respond is to pledge back, to meet a promise with a promise. From the participle ~sponsus~/~sponsa~ (“the betrothed, the promised one”) Spanish drew ~esposo~ and ~esposa~ (“husband, wife”). Strikingly, ~esposas~ also means “handcuffs,” the binding ones — the same notion of being bound by a pledge. Kin include ~respuesta~, ~responsable~, and ~corresponder~.
en.resultar:
From Latin ~resultāre~ (“to spring back, to rebound”), the frequentative of ~resilīre~ (“to leap back”), from ~re-~ (“back”) plus ~salīre~ (“to leap, to jump”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sel-~ (“to jump”). Cognate with French ~résulter~, Italian ~risultare~, and English ~result~ and ~resilient~ — the latter still carrying the sense of springing back.

The metaphor is athletic: a result is what leaps out or rebounds from a set of circumstances, the way a ball bounces off a wall. Classical Latin ~resultāre~ could even mean “to echo,” sound rebounding from a surface. From the same ~salīre~ Spanish inherited a whole leaping family: ~saltar~ (“to jump”), ~salir~ (“to go out,” originally to leap forth), ~resaltar~ (“to stand out”), ~asaltar~ (“to assault,” to leap upon), and ~sobresalir~ (“to excel,” to leap above). Every outcome, etymologically, is a little rebound.
en.saber:
From Vulgar Latin *~sapēre~, a reshaping of Latin ~sapere~ (“to taste; to have good sense, to be wise”), from Proto-Italic *~sapjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~seh₁p-~ (“to taste, to perceive”). The verb runs straight across Romance as Italian ~sapere~, French ~savoir~, and Portuguese ~saber~; English carries the same root in the borrowings ~sapient~, ~savor~, ~insipid~ (“without taste”), and ~sage~ (“wise”).

The metaphor inside the word is that of the palate: to know is to have tasted, to have discernment — the tongue standing in for the mind. Latin already ran both senses side by side, and Spanish kept the double life, since ~saber~ still means both “to know” and “to taste” (« esta sopa sabe a ajo », “this soup tastes of garlic”). From the same root grew ~sabio~ (“wise; a sage”), ~sabor~ (“flavor”), ~sabroso~ (“tasty”), ~sabiduría~ (“wisdom”), and the adjective ~sabihondo~ (“know-it-all”). Spanish neatly distinguishes ~saber~ (to know a fact) from ~conocer~ (to be acquainted with).
en.sacar:
Modern Spanish ~sacar~ descends from Old Spanish ~sacar~, but its ultimate origin is genuinely disputed. By the account Corominas favors, it comes from Gothic ~sakan~ (“to quarrel, dispute, accuse at law”), a Germanic legal term: to ~sacar~ would first have meant to obtain something by winning a lawsuit, and only later to extract or take out in general. A competing account instead links it to Medieval Latin ~saccāre~ and to ~saccus~ (“sack”) — from Greek ~sákkos~, itself a Semitic loan — imagining the act of pulling goods out of a bag. The earliest Castilian traces are Latinized forms like ~saccāre~ in tenth-century documents. Portuguese ~sacar~ (“to draw out; to draw a weapon or withdraw money”) matches the Spanish form closely, and the two languages share the ambiguity of the source.

Because the origin is unsettled, the vivid legal image — winning by litigation — should be taken as a hypothesis, not a fact. What is clear is the semantic breadth Spanish gave the verb: to take out, extract, withdraw, obtain, and figuratively to deduce (~sacar en claro~) or to snap a photo (~sacar una foto~). From it Spanish built ~sacacorchos~ (“corkscrew”), ~sacapuntas~ (“pencil sharpener”), the noun ~saca~ (“large sack; withdrawal”), and the compound ~entresacar~ (“to pick out, thin out”). The related ~sonsacar~ (“to draw information out of someone, to wheedle”) preserves almost perfectly the notion of extracting something someone would rather keep — whichever of the two etymologies proves right.
en.salir:
From Latin ~salīre~ (“to jump, leap, spring”), from Proto-Italic *~saljō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sel-~ (“to spring, jump”). The same root gave Ancient Greek ~hállomai~ (“to leap”) and, most likely, Sanskrit ~sárati~ (“flows, runs”). Through Latin and French, ~salīre~ furnished English ~salient~ and ~sally~, while its frequentative ~saltāre~ (“to leap repeatedly, dance”) gave Spanish ~saltar~ and Italian ~saltare~.

The leap became a departure. In Vulgar Latin ~salīre~ drifted from “to jump” toward “to jump out, spring forth,” and Old Spanish ~salir~ settled into the everyday “to go out, leave, exit” it has today — a spring of water still ~sale~ from the ground, keeping the old image alive. Its relatives cluster around leaping and springing: ~salto~ (“a jump”), ~saltar~, ~sobresalir~ (“to stand out,” literally to “leap above”), ~salida~ (“exit, departure”) and ~asaltar~ (“to assault,” to leap upon). English ~assault~ and ~somersault~ leap from the very same Latin verb.
en.seguir:
From Vulgar Latin *~sequēre~, a reshaping of the Latin deponent ~sequī~ (“to follow”), from Proto-Italic *~sekʷōr~, from Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). The root is deep and wide: cognate with Sanskrit ~sácate~, Ancient Greek ~hépomai~ (“I follow”), and, in the Romance line, Italian ~seguire~, French ~suivre~, and Portuguese ~seguir~. English draws on the same root through Latin borrowings like ~sequence~, ~sequel~, ~second~, and ~pursue~.

Beyond plain “to follow,” Spanish ~seguir~ took on “to continue, to keep on” — « sigo esperando », “I’m still waiting” — so the verb tracks both a person and an action through time. The prefixed compounds are especially productive: ~conseguir~ (“to obtain,” literally to follow through to the end), ~perseguir~ (“to pursue, to persecute”), ~proseguir~ (“to carry on”), and ~subsiguiente~ (“subsequent”). From the same PIE root, through other Latin stems, Spanish also inherited ~secuencia~, ~consecuencia~, ~séquito~ (“retinue”), and ~ejecutar~ (“to execute”).
en.sentir:
From Latin ~sentīre~ (“to feel, perceive, be of an opinion”), from Proto-Indo-European *~sent-~, reconstructed with the sense “to head for, go, find one’s way.” It is cognate with Italian ~sentire~, Portuguese ~sentir~ and French ~sentir~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~sense~, ~sentiment~ and ~scent~; through Germanic the root also gives English ~send~ and German ~Sinn~ (“sense, mind”) and ~senden~ (“to send”).

The semantic leap from “to go” to “to feel” is striking: to perceive was, on this reconstruction, to “find one’s way” mentally toward a thing — to discern it. Latin ~sentīre~ already spanned bodily sensation, emotion and judgment, a breadth Spanish ~sentir~ keeps (“to feel” and “to be sorry”). From the same stem come ~sentido~ (“sense, meaning”), ~sentimiento~ (“feeling”), ~sensación~ (via ~sēnsus~), ~consentir~ (“to consent”), ~presentir~ (“to have a foreboding”) and ~sensato~ (“sensible”).
en.ser:
Spanish ~ser~ descends, in its commonest forms, from Latin ~esse~ (“to be”), which reaches back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁es-~ (“to be”). That root also gave Italian ~essere~, French ~être~, and the English verb itself — ~is~ and ~am~ — as well as German ~ist~. From the Latin present ~esse~ Spanish keeps ~soy~, ~es~, and ~son~; but the paradigm is famously stitched together, and several of its everyday forms descend not from ~esse~ at all.

The present indicative (~soy~, ~eres~, ~es~, ~somos~, ~sois~, ~son~) and the imperfect (~era~, from Latin ~eram~) continue ~esse~ — though ~eres~ is a curiosity, descending from the Latin future ~eris~ (“you will be”), pressed into a present to keep it distinct from ~es~. A second donor, ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from *~sed-~, supplied the infinitive ~ser~ itself (through Old Spanish ~seer~), the future and conditional (~seré~, ~sería~), the present subjunctive (~sea~), and the imperative (~sé~) — so the very name of the verb means, etymologically, “to sit.” A third donor, the Latin perfect ~fuī~, from *~bʰuH-~ (“to become, grow”), gave the preterite (~fui~, ~fuiste~, ~fue~) — forms shared identically with ~ir~ (“to go”), so that ~fui~ means both “I was” and “I went,” context alone deciding.

From the ~esse~ / *~h₁es-~ side comes a wide family of learned words: ~ente~, ~esencia~, ~presente~, ~ausente~, and ~interés~. From ~sedēre~ (“to sit”) comes another cluster built on the idea of sitting or settling: ~sede~ (“seat, see”), ~sentar~, ~sesión~, and ~residir~. The suppletion that looks so chaotic in the paradigm is, in the vocabulary, two tidy word-families braided into one verb.
en.servir:
From Latin ~servīre~ (“to be a slave, to serve”), derived from ~servus~ (“slave, servant”). There the trail grows faint: the origin of ~servus~ is uncertain. It is usually traced to Proto-Italic *~serwos~ and compared with Umbrian ~seritu~, and it has sometimes been proposed as an Etruscan borrowing, but no account is secure, so the deeper root is best left open. The verb passed intact into Italian ~servire~, French ~servir~, and Portuguese ~servir~.

In Rome ~servīre~ meant literally to live in bondage; as that social reality faded, the word softened into today's neutral senses of waiting on someone, serving food, and — in ~servir~ para algo — simply being useful. A caution for the curious: Latin ~servāre~ (“to keep, to guard”), the source of ~conservar~ and ~observar~, springs from a different root and is not a relative, despite the resemblance. The genuine family of ~servus~ includes ~siervo~, ~servicio~, ~servil~, ~servidumbre~, and ~servidor~; its present participle ~servientem~ gave both Spanish ~sirviente~ and, by a long detour through French, English ~sergeant~.
en.señalar:
A denominative from ~señal~ (“sign, mark, signal”), which comes from Late Latin ~signālis~ (“of a sign”), from Latin ~signum~ (“mark, sign, military standard”). The root of ~signum~ is genuinely disputed: one account derives it from Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”), making a sign “something cut or carved”; another from *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow,” as in Latin ~sequī~), making it “the standard the troops follow.” The forms are cognate with Italian ~segnalare~, French ~signaler~ and English ~signal~ and ~sign~.

From ~signālis~ Spanish built the noun ~señal~ and then the verb ~señalar~, “to mark” and hence “to point out, indicate.” Because the deeper origin is unsettled, the vivid “a sign is something carved” reading should be offered only as one contested hypothesis, not as fact. The same ~signum~ radiates through Spanish: ~seña~ (“gesture, sign”), ~signo~, ~diseñar~ (“to design,” via Italian) and, most surprisingly, ~enseñar~ (“to teach”), from Latin ~īnsignāre~, literally “to mark in, imprint.”
en.solicitar:
Spanish ~solicitar~ comes from Latin ~sollicitāre~ (“to disturb, stir up, agitate”), a verb built on the adjective ~sollicitus~ (“thoroughly moved, anxious, worried”). That adjective is transparent: ~sollus~ (“whole, entire”) plus ~citus~ (“set in motion, roused”), the past participle of ~ciēre~ (“to move, stir”). ~sollus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~solh₂-~ (“whole”), the root behind Greek ~hólos~ (“whole,” as in ~holo-~) and Latin ~salvus~ (“safe”); ~ciēre~ reflects *~keyh₁-~ (“to set in motion”). English borrowed the family directly: ~solicit~, ~solicitous~, and ~solicitude~ all sit beside the Spanish verb.

The literal Latin sense was physical agitation — to shake something thoroughly, to trouble it entirely. From “to disturb, importune” the meaning softened into “to entreat, petition,” and Spanish ~solicitar~ now spans a polite request (~solicitar una beca~, “to apply for a scholarship”), a formal application, and the still-charged ~solicitar a alguien~ (“to court or proposition someone”), where the old sense of stirring another person up survives. The past participle gave ~solícito~ (“attentive, obliging”) and the noun ~solicitud~ (“request; application; solicitude”). Through the same root *~solh₂-~ Spanish also holds ~sólido~, ~salvo~, ~salud~, and ~católico~ (from Greek ~katholikós~, “universal, on the whole”).
en.sufrir:
From Old Spanish ~sofrir~, from Vulgar Latin *~sufferīre~ (a re-conjugated form), from Latin ~sufferre~ (“to bear up under, endure”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, bear”). Romance kept the compound: French ~souffrir~, Italian ~soffrire~, Portuguese ~sofrer~; English borrowed ~suffer~ through Anglo-Norman, while the same root *~bʰer-~ gives inherited English ~bear~.

The image is bodily: ~sufferre~ joins ~sub-~ (“under”) to ~ferre~ (“carry”), so to suffer is to bear a load from beneath, to hold up under weight; the sense drifted from “endure, tolerate” to “undergo pain,” though Spanish ~sufrir~ still keeps the older “put up with.” ~ferre~ was one of Latin's great verb-forges, yielding Spanish ~referir~, ~transferir~, ~preferir~, and even ~ofrecer~ (from ~offerre~), plus the adjective ~fértil~ (“bearing, fruitful”). Through *~bʰer-~ it is a cousin of English ~bear~.
en.suponer:
Spanish ~suponer~ comes from Latin ~suppōnere~ (“to place under, to substitute”), from ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, to place”). ~pōnere~ itself is a contraction of an older ~po-~ (“off, away”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, to leave”), so “to place” was originally “to set down and leave.” Because Spanish inherited ~pōnere~ as the everyday ~poner~, the compound was reshaped on it. Cognate Romance verbs include French ~supposer~ and Italian ~supporre~.

From “to place under” came the mental sense: to suppose is to lay a proposition down as a foundation to reason from — quite literally to place it beneath an argument. The Latin verb's past participle ~positus~ gave Spanish ~puesto~ (“placed; a post, position”) and spread through a large prefixed family built on ~poner~: ~componer~ (“to compose”), ~proponer~ (“to propose”), ~disponer~ (“to arrange”), ~exponer~ (“to expose”) and ~imponer~ (“to impose”), plus the nouns ~posición~ (“position”) and ~apuesta~ (“a bet,” something put down).
en.tener:
Spanish ~tener~ comes from Latin ~tenēre~ (“to hold, keep, grasp”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”) — holding conceived as keeping something taut in the hand. Its Romance cousins keep the shape: Italian ~tenere~, French ~tenir~, and Portuguese ~ter~. Through the same root, Latin also formed ~tendere~ (“to stretch”) and ~tenuis~ (“thin”), and the root even surfaces in the English ~thin~.

In Latin ~tenēre~ meant simply to hold; Spanish then handed it a much bigger job. As ~haber~ retreated into an auxiliary, ~tener~ stepped in as the ordinary verb of possession — the everyday “I have” of ~tengo hambre~ (“I hold hunger”) and ~tener casa~. The idea of holding fast runs through its descendants: ~contener~ (“to contain”), ~obtener~ (“to obtain”), ~mantener~ (“to maintain”), and the adjective ~tenaz~ (“tenacious”), along with ~teniente~ (“lieutenant,” literally one who holds a place).
en.terminar:
From Latin ~termināre~ (“to bound, to limit”), from ~terminus~ (“boundary, limit, end-marker”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ter-~ (“peg, boundary marker”), seen in the extended form *~ter-men-~. Cognate with Ancient Greek ~térma~ (“goal”) and ~térmōn~ (“border”), and with English ~term~ and ~terminal~.

For the Romans a ~terminus~ was a very concrete thing: a boundary stone set between fields. It was sacred enough to have its own god, ~Terminus~, the deity of boundary markers, honored each February at a festival called the ~Terminalia~. To ~terminar~ something, then, is etymologically to set its limit — to mark where it ends. From the same root Spanish built ~término~ (“term, end”), ~terminal~, ~determinar~ (“to bound thoroughly, to decide”), and ~exterminar~ (“to drive beyond the boundary, to destroy”).
en.tomar:
The origin of ~tomar~ is genuinely uncertain — es.Wiktionary and the DLE label it « de origen incierto ». It appears very early in Spanish (already in the medieval Poema de mio Cid) and has a close counterpart in Portuguese ~tomar~, but no agreed Latin ancestor. Two hypotheses compete. Corominas proposed an aphaeresis from Latin ~autumāre~ (“to assert a claim, affirm”), the initial ~au-~ having worn away, though the meaning fits awkwardly. Another account, associated with Walsh, derives it instead from an alteration of ~domāre~ (“to tame, subdue”), noting that early ~tomar~ worked much like ~apropiar~ (“to appropriate, take possession”). The matter remains debated, and any single story should be taken as a proposal, not settled fact.

Whatever its source, ~tomar~ established itself as one of the most versatile verbs in Spanish, spreading from “to seize, take hold of” into a vast web of senses: to take a road, take a decision, take medicine, and — famously in Spain and much of Latin America — to drink (~tomar algo~, “to have a drink”). This last is a native extension of “take into the body,” not a separate root. Reflexive ~tomarse~ intensifies it (~tomarse un café~, ~tomarse su tiempo~). Because its etymology is unsettled, ~tomar~ has left a smaller word-family than the great Latin verbs, but it did yield the nouns ~toma~ (“a taking; a dose; a film take”) and ~tomadura~, and the compound ~tomavistas~ (“a movie camera,” literally a “view-taker”). Its very obscurity is a reminder that even the commonest words can guard a hidden past.
en.trabajar:
From Old Spanish ~trabajar~ (“to toil, torment”), most often traced to a Vulgar Latin *~tripaliāre~ (“to torture”), from Late Latin ~tripalium~, a frame of three stakes (~tri-~ + ~pālus~, “stake”) used to restrain or torment. Cognate with French ~travailler~, Portuguese ~trabalhar~, Catalan ~treballar~, and Italian ~travagliare~, and with the noun French ~travail~ that gave English ~travail~ and, remarkably, ~travel~.

The oft-repeated tale is vivid — a word for “work” born from an engine of torture — but it should be told with the hedge the sources give it: while the DLE and Corominas do derive ~trabajar~ from ~tripalium~, the exact form of the Vulgar Latin verb and the precise semantic path from “torture” to “labor” remain debated, and some scholars are skeptical of the whole chain. What is clear is the drift attested in the Old Spanish records: from “to torment, suffer,” through “to strive, exert oneself,” to the neutral modern “to work.” English ~travel~ preserves the older bite, journeying once being an ordeal. The verb gave Spanish ~trabajo~ (“work”), ~trabajador~ (“worker”), and ~trabajoso~ (“laborious, arduous”).
en.tratar:
From Latin ~tractāre~ (“to drag about, handle, manage, deal with”), the frequentative of ~trahere~ (“to draw, drag, pull”), which is perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰregʰ-~ (“to draw, pull”), though ~trahere~’s deeper origin is uncertain. Cognate with Italian ~trattare~, French ~traiter~, and Portuguese ~tratar~; through the same Latin verb English acquired ~treat~, ~treaty~, and ~tract~, and through ~trahere~’s participle ~tractus~, English ~trace~, ~trait~, and ~portray~.

A frequentative names repeated or intensive action, so ~tractāre~ was “to keep dragging or handling,” and from physical handling grew the ideas of managing an affair, dealing with people, and discussing a subject — the whole spread of Spanish ~tratar~. To ~tratar a alguien~ is to treat someone (well or badly); ~tratar de~ means both “to try to” and “to be about”; and ~tratarse de~ means “to be a question of.” The inherited verb ~traer~ (“to bring”) descends from the very same ~trahere~ by the popular route, a doublet of learned ~tratar~. From this root also flow ~trato~, ~tratado~, ~tratamiento~, ~retrato~, ~contrato~, ~atraer~, and ~tracción~.
en.ubicar:
From Latin ~ubi~ (“where”), through a Late/Medieval Latin verb *~ubicāre~ and the noun ~ubicātiō~ (“a locating, position”). ~ubi~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European interrogative-relative stem *~kʷo-~ (as in ~quis~, “who”) and is parallel to Latin ~ibi~ (“there”). Unlike most Spanish verbs, ~ubicar~ was not inherited from spoken Latin but built on a Latin adverb — a learned coinage, long especially current in American Spanish.

To ubicar is, literally, to answer the question “where?” — to fix a thing’s place. From the same ~ubi~, plus the enclitic ~-que~, Latin formed ~ubīque~ (“everywhere”), which gave Spanish ~ubicuo~ (“ubiquitous”) and ~ubicuidad~; ~ubicuidad~ began life as a theological term for God’s presence everywhere. English ~ubiquitous~ descends from the same ~ubīque~, and everyday ~ubicación~ shares the verb’s root. The homely adverb “where” thus underlies a small, learned family.
en.unir:
From Latin ~ūnīre~ (“to unite, join into one”), derived from ~ūnus~ (“one”). ~ūnus~ comes from Old Latin ~oinos~, from Proto-Italic *~oinos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~óynos~ (“one, single”). The same root gave English ~one~, ~an~ and ~only~, German ~ein~, and Greek ~oínē~ (the “one” on a die). Among cognate Romance forms are Italian ~unire~, Portuguese ~unir~ and French ~unir~; English ~unite~ is a learned borrowing of the same Latin verb.

The Latin verb was built straightforwardly from the numeral: to ~unir~ is to make things ~ūnus~, one. Because the notion of oneness is so basic, its descendants spread everywhere in Spanish — ~uno~, ~unión~, ~unidad~, ~único~, ~universo~ (literally “turned into one”), ~reunir~ and ~unánime~ (“of one mind”). Even the humble ~onza~ and English ~ounce~ trace back to ~ūnus~ through ~uncia~, a “single” twelfth part. Few roots pack so much of a language’s vocabulary into one small word for “one.”
en.usar:
From Vulgar Latin ~ūsāre~, a frequentative built on ~ūsus~, the past participle of Latin ~ūtī~ (“to use, employ, make use of”). The deeper origin of ~ūtī~ is uncertain: it has been tentatively linked to Proto-Indo-European *~h₃eyt-~ (“to take along, fetch”), but the connection is disputed and far from secure. Cognate Romance descendants include Italian ~usare~, Portuguese ~usar~ and French ~user~; English ~use~ came through Old French ~user~ from the same Vulgar Latin verb.

Latin already used ~ūtī~ very broadly — to employ, enjoy, or associate with something — and the frequentative ~ūsāre~ simply meant to do so habitually, which is why Spanish ~usar~ covers everyday “using” of every kind. The participial stem ~ūsus~ is the productive one in Spanish: ~uso~, ~usar~, ~usado~, ~usuario~, ~usual~ and ~abusar~ (“to misuse”) all grow from it, as do the learned ~útil~ (“useful”) and ~utilizar~ from the related adjective ~ūtilis~. Even English ~utensil~ shares that adjective — a thing fit to be used.
en.utilizar:
A relatively modern formation, from the adjective ~útil~ (“useful”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-izar~, and closely paralleling French ~utiliser~ (whence it likely took its impulse in the nineteenth century). ~útil~ descends from Latin ~ūtilis~ (“useful, serviceable”), from ~ūtī~ (“to use, make use of”), a verb of uncertain origin with no secure Proto-Indo-European etymology. Cognate through Latin with Italian ~utilizzare~, Portuguese ~utilizar~, and English ~utilize~ and ~utility~.

The chain is short but instructive: from ~ūtī~ “to use” Latin built the adjective ~ūtilis~ “usable,” Spanish inherited it as ~útil~, and only later did the language forge a verb from the adjective with ~-izar~, giving a slightly bookish ~utilizar~ beside the older, plainer ~usar~ (from Latin ~ūsāre~, itself a frequentative of ~ūtī~ through its participle ~ūsus~). The two coexist, ~utilizar~ often carrying a shade of “to put to use, make instrumental use of.” From the same ~ūtī~ come ~útil~, ~utilidad~, ~inútil~, ~utensilio~, ~uso~, ~usar~, and ~usual~, and the borrowed ~utilitario~ (“utilitarian”).
en.vender:
From Latin ~vēndere~, a fusion of the phrase ~vēnum dare~ (“to give for sale”), from ~vēnum~ (“sale, that which is for sale”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”). ~vēnum~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~wes-~ (“to buy, sell”), and ~dare~ to *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Romance kept the compound intact: Italian ~vendere~, French ~vendre~, Portuguese ~vender~.

Latin welded a two-word phrase — “give for sale” — into a single verb, whose passive twin ~vēneō~ meant “to be sold,” literally “to go to sale.” What ~vender~ carries is a deep commercial vocabulary: the ~vēnum~ element (“price, sale”) is cognate with Ancient Greek ~ὦνος~ (“price”) and Sanskrit ~vasná~ (“price”), showing how old the idea of a fixed price is. From it Spanish keeps ~venta~ (“sale”), ~vendedor~, and ~venal~ (“that can be bought, corruptible”), while ~dare~ seeds another vast family, beginning with ~dar~ (“to give”).
en.venir:
From Latin ~venīre~ (“to come”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷeniō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to come, go, step”). This is one of the great Indo-European roots: it gave English ~come~ (through Germanic), Ancient Greek ~baínō~ (“to walk, step”) and Sanskrit ~gácchati~ (“goes”). Cognate Romance verbs include Italian ~venire~, Portuguese ~vir~ and French ~venir~; English ~venue~ is Old French ~venue~, literally “a coming.”

The Latin sense “to come” passed intact into Spanish ~venir~, and the verb’s prefixed compounds became a workshop of vocabulary in both Latin and Spanish. From ~venīre~ Spanish draws ~venida~ (“arrival”), ~porvenir~ (“future,” literally “what is to come”), ~convenir~ (“to suit, agree” — to “come together”), ~intervenir~, ~prevenir~ (“to prevent,” to “come before”) and ~aventura~ (“adventure,” from ~adventūra~, “things about to come”). Through Latin the same root reaches English ~advent~, ~convene~, ~invent~ and ~revenue~ — a striking spread from one small word for “to come.”
en.ver:
Spanish ~ver~ comes, through Old Spanish ~veer~, from Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyd-~, which meant both “to see” and “to know” — for the ancients, to have seen a thing was to know it. That double sense survives in the Germanic cousins: English ~wit~ and ~wise~, and German ~wissen~ (“to know”), all from the same root, as is Greek ~idéa~ (“form, idea”). The Romance reflexes stayed on the “see” side: French ~voir~, Italian ~vedere~.

Latin ~vidēre~ kept mainly the visual sense, and Spanish inherited it whole, down to the irregular participle ~visto~ (“seen”). The root spreads through a family of looking and seeming: ~vista~ (“sight, view”), ~visión~ (“vision”), ~evidente~ (“evident,” what is plainly seen), ~prever~ (“to foresee”), ~revisar~ (“to review”), and ~aviso~ (“notice, warning”). Modern ~vídeo~ — Latin for “I see” — joins the same ancient family, the newest branch on a very old root of seeing.
en.vivir:
From Latin ~vīvere~ (“to live”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷīwō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷeyh₃-~ (“to live”). The root is deeply Indo-European: it gave Old English ~cwic~ (“alive”), source of modern English ~quick~ (which once meant “living,” as in “the quick and the dead”), and Ancient Greek ~bíos~ (“life”). Cognate Romance verbs include Italian ~vivere~, Portuguese ~viver~ and French ~vivre~; English ~vivid~ and ~revive~ borrow the Latin verb directly.

Latin ~vīvere~ meant simply “to be alive,” and Spanish ~vivir~ inherited both that and the richer “to dwell, to spend one’s life.” Its family is full of life in every sense: ~vida~ (“life,” from ~vīta~), ~vivo~ (“alive, lively”), ~vívido~, ~vitalidad~, ~convivir~ (“to live together”), ~sobrevivir~ (“to survive,” to “over-live”) and ~víveres~ (“provisions,” the things that keep one living).
